subtopics.title: Counting principles and the binomial theorem for rational indices
subtopics.guide: Counting principles (multiplication and addition rules), permutations and combinations of distinct objects, with arrangements of identical objects and circular arrangements excluded. Extends the binomial theorem to (a + b)^n for rational n, written as a^n(1 + b/a)^n, as an infinite series valid for |b/a| < 1 and used for approximations; proof of the theorem is not required.

skills.name: Count outcomes with the multiplication and addition principles
examTypes: How many four-digit numbers can be made with no repeated digits?
A code is two letters followed by three digits; find the number of possible codes
Find how many even three-digit numbers can be made from the digits 1 to 6 without repetition
A menu offers 4 starters, 5 mains and 3 desserts; count the meals with a starter or a dessert (or both) and a main

methods.name: Fill the slots and multiply
methods.summary: Draw one box per position, write the number of choices in each (most restricted box first), then multiply: 9 × 9 × 8 × 7 = 4536 four-digit numbers with no repeats.

methods.name: Split into disjoint cases and add
methods.summary: When choices depend on an earlier choice, split into cases (for example by the last digit) that cannot happen together, count each with the product rule and add.

methods.name: Count everything, then subtract the bad cases
methods.summary: Total arrangements minus those that break the rule, for example all digit strings minus those starting with 0.

methods.name: Draw a tree for small cases
methods.summary: List the branches stage by stage; the number of end points is the product of the branch counts, which also shows why the rule is multiplication.

misconceptions: Ignoring the leading-zero restriction: 10 × 9 × 8 × 7 = 5040 four-digit numbers instead of 4536
Adding when the stages happen together: 26 + 26 + 10 + 10 + 10 = 82 codes instead of 26² × 10³ = 676 000
Filling the unrestricted slots first and then assuming 3 even digits remain: 6 × 5 × 3 = 90 even three-digit numbers instead of 3 × 5 × 4 = 60

threads.echo: Each extra digit multiplies the number of codes by 10, so the count of n-digit strings, 10^n, is a geometric sequence in n.

skills.name: Count ordered arrangements with n! and nPr
examTypes: In how many ways can 7 different books be arranged on a shelf?
A gold, silver and bronze are awarded among 10 runners; find the number of possible results
Find n given that nP2 = 56
Show that nPr = n!/(n − r)!

methods.name: Use nPr = n!/(n − r)!
methods.summary: 10P3 = 10!/7! = 10 × 9 × 8 = 720; cancel the factorials rather than evaluating them.

methods.name: Multiply the falling choices
methods.summary: The first place has 10 choices, the second 9, the third 8: the same product as nPr, built from the counting principle.

methods.name: Use the nPr function on the GDC
methods.summary: Enter 10 nPr 3, or tabulate xP2 to find which n gives 56.

methods.name: Turn nPr into a polynomial in n
methods.summary: nP2 = n(n − 1) = 56 gives n² − n − 56 = 0, so n = 8 (reject n = −7).

misconceptions: Using combinations when order matters: 10C3 = 120 medal results instead of 720
Allowing repeats: 10³ = 1000 medal results, as if one runner could win two medals
Writing nPr = n!/r! (for 10P3 this gives 10!/3! = 604 800)

threads.echo: nPr = nCr × r!, because each choice of r objects can be put in order in r! ways; dividing out the order gives the nCr in Pascal's triangle.

skills.name: Count selections with nCr, including 'at least' and mixed-group conditions
examTypes: A committee of 4 is chosen from 6 men and 5 women; how many committees contain exactly 2 women?
Find the number of committees with at least one woman
How many ways can a team of 5 be chosen from 12 players if the captain must be included?
Find the number of lines determined by 8 points, no three of which are collinear

methods.name: Choose from each group and multiply
methods.summary: Exactly 2 women and 2 men: 5C2 × 6C2 = 10 × 15 = 150.

methods.name: Use the complement for 'at least one'
methods.summary: All committees minus those with no women: 11C4 − 6C4 = 330 − 15 = 315.

methods.name: Add the cases one by one
methods.summary: Sum the committees with 1, 2, 3 and 4 women: 100 + 150 + 60 + 5 = 315, a check on the complement.

methods.name: Fix the forced members first
methods.summary: If the captain must play, choose the other 4 from the remaining 11: 11C4 = 330.

methods.name: Evaluate nCr on the GDC
methods.summary: Use n nCr r for large values and to check hand calculations.

misconceptions: Adding instead of multiplying across groups: 5C2 + 6C2 = 25 instead of 150
Counting 'at least one woman' as 5 × 10C3 = 600, which counts committees with several women more than once (true answer 315)
Using 11P4 = 7920 for a committee, where order does not matter

threads.echo: 5C2 × 6C2 ÷ 11C4 is the probability that a random committee has exactly 2 women; the same nCr numbers fill Pascal's triangle and the coefficients of (a + b)^n.
Choosing the 4 people who serve is the same as choosing the 7 who do not, so 11C4 = 11C7.

skills.name: Count arrangements with conditions (together, apart, fixed positions)
examTypes: Six people sit in a row; in how many ways can two particular people sit next to each other?
Find the number of arrangements in which they are not next to each other
How many arrangements of the letters of FRIDAY begin and end with a vowel?
In how many orders can 6 runners finish if A finishes ahead of B?

methods.name: Treat the pair as one block
methods.summary: Glue A and B into one unit: 5! arrangements of 5 units, times 2! orders inside the block, gives 240.

methods.name: Subtract the 'together' cases from the total
methods.summary: Not together = 6! − 240 = 480.

methods.name: Arrange the others, then place into gaps
methods.summary: Arrange the other 4 people (4! = 24), then put A and B into 2 of the 5 gaps in order (5P2 = 20): 480.

methods.name: Use symmetry between A and B
methods.summary: Swapping A and B pairs each arrangement with A ahead with one with B ahead, so exactly half of 6! = 720, that is 360, have A ahead.

misconceptions: Forgetting the 2! inside the block: 5! = 120 arrangements with A and B together instead of 240
Counting 'apart' as 6! − 2 = 718, subtracting only two arrangements
Allowing the same vowel at both ends of FRIDAY: 2 × 2 × 4! = 96 instead of 2! × 4! = 48

threads.echo: A ahead of B in exactly half the arrangements is the same 'swap gives a match' argument behind nCr = nC(n − r).

skills.name: Expand (a + b)^n for negative or fractional n and state the interval of validity
examTypes: Find the first four terms of the expansion of (1 + x)^(−1/2) in ascending powers of x
Expand (2 + x)^(−1) up to the term in x², stating the values of x for which it is valid
Find the coefficient of x³ in the expansion of (1 − 3x)^(1/3)
The first two terms of (1 + ax)^n are 1 − 6x and the coefficient of x² is 27; find a and n

methods.name: Use 1 + nx + n(n − 1)x²/2! + n(n − 1)(n − 2)x³/3! + …
methods.summary: For n = −1/2: 1 − x/2 + 3x²/8 − 5x³/16 + …, valid for |x| < 1; brackets round the whole x-term when x is replaced by −3x or x/2.

methods.name: Check against a geometric series
methods.summary: For n = −1, (1 − x)^(−1) = 1 + x + x² + … is the geometric series with ratio x, which confirms both the coefficients and the condition |x| < 1.

methods.name: Equate coefficients to find unknowns
methods.summary: From na = −6 and n(n − 1)a²/2 = 27, eliminate a: (n − 1)/n = 54/36, so n = −2 and a = 3.

misconceptions: Factoring a out without the power: (4 + x)^(1/2) = 4(1 + x/4)^(1/2) instead of 2(1 + x/4)^(1/2)
Giving the validity of (2 + x)^(−1) as |x| < 1 instead of |x| < 2
Not bracketing the substituted term: writing the x² term of (1 − 3x)^(1/3) as −(1/9)(3x²) = −x²/3 instead of −(1/9)(−3x)² = −x²
Trying to use nCr with negative n, or expecting the expansion to stop after n + 1 terms

threads.echo: The coefficients n(n − 1)…(n − r + 1)/r! are exactly nCr when n is a positive integer; for other n the same pattern continues forever.
Rewriting (a + b)^n as a^n(1 + b/a)^n changes nothing about the value but reveals the form the series needs and its range of validity.
(1 − x)^(−1) is the sum of a geometric series with ratio x, which converges only when |x| < 1.

skills.name: Use a binomial series to approximate a value
examTypes: Use the expansion of (1 + x)^(1/2) to find an approximation to √1.02
By substituting a suitable value of x, use the expansion of (1 − x)^(1/2) to approximate √3 as a fraction
Explain why x = 3 cannot be substituted to approximate √4
Find the percentage error of the approximation

methods.name: Substitute a small x into the truncated series
Rescale so that x is small
Compare with the GDC value
methods.summary: Evaluate the true value to find the error, or tabulate partial sums to see them settle.

methods.name: Use the size of the next term
methods.summary: The first omitted term gives a rough size for the error when x is small.

misconceptions: Substituting a value outside the interval of validity: x = 3 in (1 + x)^(1/2) gives 1 + 1.5 − 1.125 = 1.375, nowhere near √4 = 2
Substituting x = 1.02 instead of x = 0.02 to approximate √1.02
Forgetting the factor outside: √3 ≈ (1 − 1/4)^(1/2) ≈ 0.867 rather than 2 × 0.867

threads.echo: The approximation adds up ever smaller pieces of an infinite series, and stops when the next piece is too small to matter.

subtopics.title: Partial fractions
subtopics.guide: Split a proper rational expression into partial fractions when the denominator has at most two distinct linear factors (degree of numerator less than that of the denominator). Repeated factors, irreducible quadratic factors and improper fractions are outside this statement; the main use is rearranging integrands in AHL5.15.

skills.name: Split (px + q)/((x − a)(x − b)) into partial fractions
examTypes: Express (5x + 1)/((x − 1)(x + 2)) in partial fractions
Given that (x + 5)/((x + 1)(x − 3)) ≡ A/(x + 1) + B/(x − 3), find A and B
Write 3/((2x + 1)(x − 1)) in the form A/(2x + 1) + B/(x − 1)

methods.name: Clear denominators and substitute the roots
methods.summary: 5x + 1 ≡ A(x + 2) + B(x − 1); x = 1 gives 6 = 3A so A = 2, and x = −2 gives −9 = −3B so B = 3.

methods.name: Equate coefficients
methods.summary: Compare x terms and constants: A + B = 5 and 2A − B = 1, then solve simultaneously.

methods.name: Cover-up rule
methods.summary: For A, cover (x − 1) in the original and put x = 1 into what is left: (5 + 1)/(1 + 2) = 2; similarly for B.

misconceptions: Substituting the wrong root for a non-monic factor: using x = −1 instead of x = −1/2 for (2x + 1)
Sign slip when substituting: x = −2 in B(x − 1) taken as B(1), giving B = −9 instead of 3
Writing the numerator identity as 5x + 1 ≡ A(x − 1) + B(x + 2), pairing each constant with its own factor (gives A = 3, B = 2 swapped)

threads.echo: (5x + 1)/((x − 1)(x + 2)) and 2/(x − 1) + 3/(x + 2) are the same function; the split form is the one you can integrate or sum term by term.

skills.name: Factorise a quadratic denominator, then split into partial fractions
examTypes: Express (x + 8)/(x² + x − 6) in partial fractions
Write 1/(x² − 4) as the sum of two fractions with linear denominators
Express (7x + 3)/(2x² + x − 3) in partial fractions

methods.name: Equate coefficients after factorising
methods.summary: A + B = 1 and −2A + 3B = 8 give the same A = −1, B = 2.

misconceptions: Factorising x² + x − 6 as (x − 3)(x + 2), which leads to the wrong roots and wrong constants
Splitting 1/(x² − 4) as 1/x² − 1/4
For 2x² + x − 3 = (2x + 3)(x − 1), substituting x = −3 instead of x = −3/2

threads.echo: Factorising the denominator is the first change of form; partial fractions is the second, and each exposes a different feature.

skills.name: Recombine or check a partial-fraction identity
examTypes: A student claims (3x + 1)/((x + 1)(x − 1)) ≡ 1/(x + 1) + 2/(x − 1); verify or correct
Check your partial fractions by substituting x = 0

methods.name: Test a convenient value of x
methods.summary: At x = 0 the claimed identity gives −1 on the left and 1 − 2 = −1 on the right; agreement at one value is a check, not a proof.

methods.name: Graph both sides
methods.summary: If the two graphs coincide everywhere they are defined, the identity is plausible.

misconceptions: Adding numerators and denominators separately: 1/(x − 1) − 1/(x + 1) = 0/(−2) = 0
Treating agreement at a single value of x as a proof of the identity
Combining 1/(x + 1) + 2/(x − 1) as (1 + 2)/((x + 1)(x − 1)) = 3/(x² − 1), forgetting to multiply each numerator by the other factor

threads.echo: Splitting into partial fractions undoes adding two fractions over a common denominator, so recombining is the natural check.

subtopics.title: Complex numbers in Cartesian form and the complex plane
subtopics.guide: The imaginary unit i with i² = −1, complex numbers in Cartesian form a + bi, and the vocabulary of real part, imaginary part, conjugate, modulus and argument. Includes arithmetic in Cartesian form and representing complex numbers as points or vectors in the complex plane (Argand diagram).

skills.name: Simplify powers of i
examTypes: Simplify i^27
Find the value of i + i² + i³ + i⁴
Simplify (2i)⁵
Write √(−49) in terms of i

methods.name: Use the cycle i, −1, −i, 1
methods.summary: Powers of i repeat every 4; 27 = 4 × 6 + 3, so i^27 = i³ = −i.

methods.name: Count quarter turns on the Argand diagram
methods.summary: Each factor of i rotates 90° anticlockwise; 27 quarter turns is 6 full turns plus three quarters, landing on −i.

misconceptions: Taking i³ = i (it is −i), so i^27 is given as i
Writing (2i)⁵ = 2i⁵ = 2i instead of 32i
Writing √(−49) = −7 or 7i² instead of 7i

threads.echo: Repeated multiplication by i does not grow the number; it rotates it, so the powers cycle with period 4.

skills.name: Add, subtract, multiply and divide complex numbers in Cartesian form
examTypes: Find (3 + 2i)(1 − i) in the form a + bi
Express (2 + 3i)/(1 − i) in the form a + bi
Given z = 1 + 2i, find z² − 2z
Find the real number k for which (k + i)(2 − 3i) is real

methods.name: Multiply top and bottom by the conjugate
Use complex mode on the GDC
methods.summary: On Paper 2, enter the expression directly in a + bi mode to compute or check.

methods.name: Convert to polar form for products and quotients
methods.summary: Multiply moduli and add arguments (AHL1.13), useful for high powers or awkward quotients.

misconceptions: Using i² = +1: (3 + 2i)(1 − i) = 1 − i instead of 5 − i
Multiplying only the denominator by the conjugate, giving (2 + 3i)/2
Multiplying parts pairwise: (3 + 2i)(1 − i) = 3 − 2i, losing the cross terms

threads.echo: Realising the denominator rewrites a quotient as a + bi without changing its value, just as rationalising a surd does.

skills.name: Find the real and imaginary parts, conjugate, modulus and argument
examTypes: For z = 3 − 4i, write down Re(z), Im(z) and z*
Find |−1 + √3 i| and arg(−1 + √3 i)
Show that z z* = |z|² for z = a + bi
Find the argument of −2 − 2i in the interval −π < θ ≤ π

methods.name: |z| = √(a² + b²), then arctan with quadrant check
methods.summary: For −1 + √3 i: |z| = 2; the reference angle is arctan √3 = π/3, and the point is in the second quadrant, so arg z = 2π/3.

methods.name: Sketch the point before finding the angle
methods.summary: Plot (a, b) on the Argand diagram to see the quadrant, then find the angle from the positive real axis.

methods.name: Use abs() and angle() on the GDC
methods.summary: The GDC returns the modulus and the principal argument directly; check the mode is radians.

misconceptions: Giving Im(3 − 4i) as −4i instead of −4
Taking arg(−1 + √3 i) = arctan(√3/−1) = −π/3 without correcting for the quadrant (it is 2π/3)
Finding |3 − 4i| as 3 + 4 = 7, or as √(9 − 16), instead of 5
Writing the conjugate of 3 − 4i as −3 + 4i instead of 3 + 4i

threads.echo: The modulus of a + bi is the length of the vector (a, b), found by Pythagoras exactly like a vector magnitude.
The conjugate is the reflection of z in the real axis, so it has the same modulus and the opposite argument.

skills.name: Solve equations by equating real and imaginary parts
examTypes: Find z = x + iy such that z + 2z* = 6 − i
Find the square roots of 3 + 4i in the form a + bi
Find real a and b such that (a + bi)(2 − i) = 7 + 4i
Solve 2z − iz* = 3 for z

methods.name: Write z = x + iy and equate parts
methods.summary: z + 2z* = 3x − iy = 6 − i, so x = 2, y = 1 and z = 2 + i.

methods.name: Set (a + bi)² equal and solve the pair
methods.summary: a² − b² = 3 and 2ab = 4; substituting b = 2/a gives a⁴ − 3a² − 4 = 0, so a² = 4 and the roots are ±(2 + i).

methods.name: Divide when the unknown appears once
Use polar form for square roots
methods.summary: Halve the argument and take the square root of the modulus (see AHL1.14), useful when a and b are not integers.

misconceptions: Giving the square root of 3 + 4i as √3 + 2i, taking square roots of each part
Giving only 2 + i and missing −(2 + i)
Forgetting that z* changes the sign of the imaginary part, so z + 2z* is treated as 3z and z = 2 − i/3

threads.echo: Two complex numbers are equal exactly when their real parts agree and their imaginary parts agree, turning one complex equation into two real ones.

skills.name: Represent complex numbers and their sums on the complex plane
examTypes: Plot z, z* and −z on an Argand diagram for z = 2 + 3i
Show z₁, z₂ and z₁ + z₂ on an Argand diagram and describe the shape formed with 0
Find the distance between the points representing 1 + 2i and 4 − 2i
Which diagram shows iz?

methods.name: Plot a + bi at (a, b)
methods.summary: Real part across, imaginary part up; z* is the reflection in the real axis and −z the half-turn about 0.

methods.name: Add as vectors
methods.summary: z₁ + z₂ is the fourth vertex of the parallelogram on 0, z₁ and z₂; z₂ − z₁ is the vector from z₁ to z₂.

misconceptions: Plotting a + bi at (b, a)
Reflecting in the imaginary axis to get z*, so 2 + 3i goes to −2 + 3i
Finding the distance as |z₁| − |z₂| = √5 − √20 rather than |z₂ − z₁| = 5

threads.echo: A complex number is a movement 'a across, b up'; adding complex numbers is adding displacement vectors head to tail.
z and z* are mirror images in the real axis, which is why their sum is real and their product is |z|².

subtopics.title: Modulus-argument and Euler forms of complex numbers
subtopics.guide: Write complex numbers in modulus-argument form r(cos θ + i sin θ) = r cis θ and Euler form re^(iθ), and convert freely between these and Cartesian form. Carry out sums, products and quotients in any form and interpret them geometrically (multiplying moduli and adding arguments as an enlargement and rotation).

skills.name: Convert between Cartesian, polar and Euler forms
examTypes: Write 1 − i in the form re^(iθ)
Express 4 cis(5π/6) in the form a + bi
Write −3 in modulus-argument form
Match each complex number to its Euler form

methods.name: Find r and θ, then write r cis θ or re^(iθ)
methods.summary: For 1 − i: r = √2 and the point is in the fourth quadrant, so θ = −π/4 and 1 − i = √2 e^(−iπ/4).

methods.name: Expand r(cos θ + i sin θ) with exact values
Sketch on the Argand diagram
methods.summary: Points on an axis can be read straight off: −3 is 3 units at angle π, so −3 = 3e^(iπ).

methods.name: Use the GDC conversion functions
methods.summary: Convert to polar and back on the GDC to check, keeping the mode in radians.

misconceptions: Giving arg(−1 − i) as π/4 from arctan(1) instead of −3π/4
Taking r = 2 for 1 − i by adding the parts instead of √2
Writing −3 as −3 cis 0, with a negative modulus, instead of 3 cis π

threads.echo: a + bi, r cis θ and re^(iθ) are one number in three notations: Cartesian is best for adding, polar and Euler for multiplying.

skills.name: Multiply and divide in polar or Euler form
examTypes: Find z₁z₂ and z₁/z₂ for z₁ = 6 cis(π/3) and z₂ = 2 cis(π/12)
Given |z₁| = 3 and arg z₁ = 2π/3, find |z₁²| and arg z₁² in the interval (−π, π]
Find |z| and arg z for z = (1 + i)/(√3 − i)
Express 2e^(iπ/4) × 3e^(−iπ/2) in Cartesian form

methods.name: Multiply moduli and add arguments
methods.summary: z₁/z₂ = (6/2) cis(π/3 − π/12) = 3 cis(π/4); for a product add the arguments instead.

methods.name: Use index laws in Euler form
Do the arithmetic in Cartesian form
methods.summary: Multiply or divide as a + bi and convert at the end; slower for quotients but a good check.

methods.name: Bring the argument back into the principal range
methods.summary: 2 × 2π/3 = 4π/3 is outside (−π, π], so subtract 2π to give −2π/3.

misconceptions: Multiplying the arguments: 6 cis(π/3) × 2 cis(π/12) = 12 cis(π²/36)
Adding the moduli: |z₁z₂| = 6 + 2 = 8 instead of 12
Dividing the arguments for a quotient: arg(z₁/z₂) = (π/3)/(π/12) = 4

threads.echo: e^(iα) × e^(iβ) = e^(i(α + β)) is the same index law as a^m × a^n = a^(m + n).
Multiplying by r cis θ stretches every point by factor r and rotates it by θ about the origin.

skills.name: Interpret multiplication and addition geometrically on the Argand diagram
examTypes: Describe the transformation that maps z onto 2iz
The point A represents z; find the complex number representing A after a rotation of π/3 anticlockwise about the origin
Show that 0, z and z e^(iπ/3) form an equilateral triangle
Which diagram shows z₁z₂ given z₁ and z₂?

methods.name: Read the multiplier as a rotation and enlargement
methods.summary: 2i = 2e^(iπ/2), so z ↦ 2iz is a rotation by π/2 anticlockwise about 0 and an enlargement with scale factor 2.

methods.name: Use the parallelogram for sums
methods.summary: z₁ + z₂ is the diagonal of the parallelogram on z₁ and z₂ from the origin.

methods.name: Check with moduli and arguments
methods.summary: |z e^(iπ/3)| = |z| and the angle between them is π/3, which with |z − z e^(iπ/3)| = |z| proves the triangle is equilateral.

misconceptions: Multiplying by i as a clockwise rotation, sending 1 + i to 1 − i instead of −1 + i
Describing multiplication by 2i as a rotation only, forgetting the enlargement by 2
Thinking adding z₂ rotates z₁, rather than translating it by the vector z₂

threads.echo: Adding a complex number is a translation, multiplying is a rotation with an enlargement: the same transformation vocabulary as for graphs.
Adding z₂ moves every point by the same vector, exactly like translating a graph by (a, b).

skills.name: Simplify sums of complex numbers in Euler or polar form
examTypes: Show that e^(iθ) + e^(−iθ) = 2 cos θ
Show that 1 + e^(iθ) = 2 cos(θ/2) e^(iθ/2) and hence find |1 + e^(iθ)| for 0 ≤ θ < π
Find the modulus and argument of cis(π/3) + cis(π/6)
Write e^(iθ) − e^(−iθ) in terms of sin θ

methods.name: Factor out the half-angle
methods.summary: 1 + e^(iθ) = e^(iθ/2)(e^(−iθ/2) + e^(iθ/2)) = 2 cos(θ/2) e^(iθ/2), so the modulus is 2 cos(θ/2) and the argument θ/2.

methods.name: Convert to Cartesian and use trig identities
methods.summary: 1 + cos θ + i sin θ; use 1 + cos θ = 2cos²(θ/2) and sin θ = 2 sin(θ/2) cos(θ/2) to reach the same result.

methods.name: Use the rhombus on the Argand diagram
methods.summary: 1 and e^(iθ) both have modulus 1, so their sum is the diagonal of a rhombus, which bisects the angle θ.

misconceptions: Adding moduli: |1 + e^(iθ)| = 2 for all θ
Adding exponents: e^(iα) + e^(iβ) = e^(i(α + β))
Writing e^(iθ) − e^(−iθ) = 2 sin θ instead of 2i sin θ

threads.echo: e^(iθ) and e^(−iθ) are mirror images in the real axis, so their imaginary parts cancel and the sum is real.
The same sum written in Cartesian form needs half-angle identities; in Euler form a single factor does the job.

skills.name: Find exact trigonometric values by comparing two forms of a product or quotient
examTypes: Find (1 + √3 i)(1 − i) in Cartesian and in polar form; hence find the exact value of cos(π/12)
By writing (√3 + i)/(1 + i) in two ways, find sin(π/12)
Hence show that tan(π/12) = 2 − √3

methods.name: Equate real parts of the two forms
Check with a compound-angle identity
methods.summary: cos(π/3 − π/4) = cos(π/3)cos(π/4) + sin(π/3)sin(π/4) gives the same (√6 + √2)/4.

misconceptions: Using modulus 2 instead of 2 × √2 for the product, giving cos(π/12) = (1 + √3)/2 > 1
Subtracting arguments for a product: arg = π/3 − (−π/4) = 7π/12
Not rationalising and so failing to match the required form (√6 + √2)/4

threads.echo: One number, two forms: matching the real parts of a + bi and r cis θ turns complex arithmetic into a trig identity.

subtopics.title: Conjugate roots, De Moivre's theorem, powers and roots of complex numbers
subtopics.guide: Non-real roots of polynomial equations with real coefficients come in conjugate pairs. De Moivre's theorem (r cis θ)^n = r^n cis nθ, proved by induction for positive integers n and known to hold more widely, is used for powers, nth roots of complex numbers (including roots of unity) and rational exponents.

skills.name: Solve quadratic equations with complex roots
examTypes: Solve z² + 2z + 5 = 0
Solve z² − 6z + 13 = 0, giving the roots in the form a ± bi
Find a quadratic with real coefficients that has a root 3 − 2i
Show the roots of a quadratic on an Argand diagram

methods.name: Build from the sum and product of the roots
methods.summary: 3 ± 2i have sum 6 and product 9 + 4 = 13, giving z² − 6z + 13 = 0.

methods.name: Use the GDC polynomial solver in complex mode
methods.summary: On Paper 2 the solver returns both complex roots directly.

misconceptions: Writing √(−16) = −4, so the roots become real: −1 ± (−2)
Dividing only the square-root term by 2: z = −2 ± 2i
Building the quadratic as z² + 6z + 13 from roots 3 ± 2i (sign of the sum wrong)

threads.echo: The roots −1 ± 2i sit symmetrically about the real axis, centred on the line of symmetry z = −1 of the parabola.
A negative discriminant means the graph never meets the x-axis, yet the algebra still gives two (complex) roots.

skills.name: Use the conjugate root theorem to factorise polynomials and find unknown coefficients
examTypes: Given that 2 − i is a root of z³ − 5z² + 9z − 5 = 0, find the other roots
Given that 1 + i is a root of z⁴ + az³ + bz² + 4z + 4 = 0 with a, b real, find a and b
Explain why a cubic with real coefficients must have at least one real root
A quartic with real coefficients has roots 2i and 3 + i; write it in factorised form

methods.name: Form the quadratic factor and divide
methods.summary: Roots 2 ± i give z² − 4z + 5; dividing z³ − 5z² + 9z − 5 by it leaves z − 1, so the third root is 1.

methods.name: Substitute the root and equate parts
methods.summary: Put z = 1 + i into the polynomial, set real and imaginary parts to zero and solve for the unknown coefficients.

methods.name: Use the sum and product of roots
methods.summary: With AHL2.12, the sum of roots of z³ − 5z² + 9z − 5 is 5 and (2 + i) + (2 − i) = 4, so the third root is 1.

methods.name: Check with the GDC polynomial solver
methods.summary: On Paper 2, solve the polynomial in complex mode to confirm all roots.

misconceptions: Taking the conjugate of 2 − i to be −2 + i or −2 − i instead of 2 + i
Forming the factor as z² + 4z + 5 for roots 2 ± i (wrong sign of the sum)
Applying the conjugate root theorem to a polynomial with non-real coefficients, such as z² − iz + 2

threads.echo: Real coefficients force the roots to be symmetric in the real axis: if z is a root, so is its mirror image z*.

skills.name: Raise complex numbers to powers with De Moivre's theorem
examTypes: Find (1 + i)^8
Find (1 + √3 i)^6 in the form a + bi
Find the smallest positive integer n for which (√3 + i)^n is real
Find the value of (cis(π/9))^12

methods.name: Convert to polar form and apply De Moivre
Set the argument condition
methods.summary: (√3 + i)^n = 2^n cis(nπ/6) is real when nπ/6 is a multiple of π, so n = 6.

methods.name: Evaluate on the GDC
methods.summary: On Paper 2, compute the power directly in complex mode; small rounding errors may show up as tiny imaginary parts.

misconceptions: Raising the modulus but not multiplying the argument: (2 cis(π/3))^6 = 64 cis(π/3)
Multiplying the modulus by n instead of raising it: (√2)^8 taken as 8√2 instead of 16
Applying the power to each part: (1 + i)^8 = 1 + i^8 = 2

threads.echo: Each multiplication by r cis θ multiplies the modulus by r and adds θ to the argument, so the powers spiral out geometrically when r > 1.
z^n repeats the same rotation-and-enlargement n times.

skills.name: Prove De Moivre's theorem for positive integers by induction
examTypes: Prove by mathematical induction that (cos θ + i sin θ)^n = cos nθ + i sin nθ for all n ∈ ℤ+
Identify the error in a given inductive step
Use the result for positive n to show it also holds for n = −1

methods.name: Induction using compound-angle identities
methods.summary: Assume true for n = k; multiply (cos kθ + i sin kθ)(cos θ + i sin θ), expand and use the cos and sin addition formulae to get cos(k + 1)θ + i sin(k + 1)θ.

methods.name: Induction using the polar product rule
methods.summary: If the product rule cis α × cis β = cis(α + β) has already been established, the inductive step is cis kθ × cis θ = cis(k + 1)θ.

misconceptions: Assuming the n = k + 1 statement in order to prove it
Expanding (cos kθ + i sin kθ)(cos θ + i sin θ) and losing the i² = −1 sign, giving cos kθ cos θ + sin kθ sin θ = cos(k − 1)θ as the real part
Omitting the base case or the concluding sentence

threads.echo: The inductive step is a 'rewrite until it matches' chain: expanding the product and recognising cos A cos B − sin A sin B as cos(A + B).

skills.name: Use De Moivre's theorem to derive multiple-angle and power identities
examTypes: Use De Moivre's theorem to show that cos 3θ = 4cos³θ − 3cos θ
Given z = cis θ, show that z^n + z^(−n) = 2cos nθ
Hence express cos³θ in terms of cos 3θ and cos θ
Express sin 3θ in terms of sin θ

methods.name: Expand (cos θ + i sin θ)^n binomially and equate parts
methods.summary: The real part of (c + is)³ is c³ − 3cs²; with s² = 1 − c² this is 4c³ − 3c = cos 3θ.

methods.name: Use z + 1/z = 2 cos θ
methods.summary: (z + 1/z)³ = z³ + 1/z³ + 3(z + 1/z), so 8cos³θ = 2cos 3θ + 6cos θ and cos³θ = (cos 3θ + 3cos θ)/4.

methods.name: Check with compound-angle identities
methods.summary: cos 3θ = cos(2θ + θ) expanded with double-angle formulae gives the same result, a useful check.

misconceptions: Forgetting the binomial coefficients: real part of (c + is)³ taken as c³ − s³
Writing z^n − z^(−n) = 2 sin nθ instead of 2i sin nθ
Losing the sign from i² when collecting terms, giving cos 3θ = 4cos³θ + 3cos θ

threads.echo: The 1, 3, 3, 1 coefficients of Pascal's triangle appear inside cos 3θ and sin 3θ.
(cis θ)³ and cis 3θ are the same number; expanding one and simplifying the other gives a trig identity for free.

skills.name: Find nth roots of a complex number, including roots of unity
examTypes: Solve z³ = 8i, giving the roots in Cartesian form
Find the fifth roots of unity and show them on an Argand diagram
Show that the sum of the nth roots of unity is zero
Find all values of (−16)^(1/4)

methods.name: Write w with a general argument and divide by n
methods.summary: 8i = 8 cis(π/2 + 2kπ), so z = 2 cis(π/6 + 2kπ/3) for k = 0, 1, 2: √3 + i, −√3 + i and −2i.

methods.name: Use the regular polygon
methods.summary: The n roots lie on a circle of radius |w|^(1/n), equally spaced by 2π/n, so one root gives all the others by rotation.

methods.name: Sum the roots as a geometric series
Factorise for small cases
methods.summary: z³ − 1 = (z − 1)(z² + z + 1), then solve the quadratic for the two non-real cube roots of unity.

misconceptions: Giving only the principal root, for example √3 + i alone for z³ = 8i
Dividing the modulus by n instead of taking the nth root: modulus 8/3 instead of 2
Dividing π/2 by 3 but adding 2kπ (not 2kπ/3) between roots, so every 'root' is the same number

threads.echo: Taking an nth root undoes raising to the power n, but, like arcsin, the undo has several answers and you must find all n.
The nth roots form a regular n-gon, so their rotational symmetry makes their sum zero.

subtopics.title: Proof by induction, by contradiction and by counterexample
subtopics.guide: Proof by mathematical induction (for example sums of series, divisibility, derivatives and complex numbers), proof by contradiction (for example irrationality results and the infinitude of primes), and disproof by a counterexample, where the student must show why the example breaks the statement rather than just stating it.

skills.name: Prove a summation formula by induction
examTypes: Prove by induction that Σ from r = 1 to n of r² = n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6
Prove that 1 × 2 + 2 × 3 + … + n(n + 1) = n(n + 1)(n + 2)/3 for n ∈ ℤ+
Put the steps of an induction proof in order
Identify what is wrong with a given inductive step

methods.name: Assume for k, add the (k + 1)th term, factorise
methods.summary: Show P(1); assume Σ up to k is the formula; add (k + 1)², take out the common factor (k + 1)/6 and reach (k + 1)(k + 2)(2k + 3)/6; conclude.

methods.name: Expand the target and the result and compare
methods.summary: If factorising is hard, expand both your result and the formula with n = k + 1 and show they are the same polynomial.

misconceptions: Checking n = 1, 2, 3 and calling it a proof
Assuming the n = k + 1 formula is true and working from it
Adding the wrong next term, k² instead of (k + 1)²
Omitting the conclusion that P(1) and P(k) ⇒ P(k + 1) give the result for all n ∈ ℤ+

threads.echo: The inductive step is 'the sum so far plus one more piece', the same build-up behind S_n and the definite integral.
The key step rewrites the sum into a factorised form that matches the target: a chain of equivalent expressions.

skills.name: Prove a divisibility result by induction
examTypes: Prove by induction that 7^n − 1 is divisible by 6 for all n ∈ ℤ+
Prove that n³ − n is divisible by 3 for all positive integers n
Prove that 5^n + 3 is divisible by 4 for all n ∈ ℤ+

methods.name: Induction: rewrite f(k + 1) using f(k)
methods.summary: Assume 7^k − 1 = 6m; then 7^(k + 1) − 1 = 7(7^k − 1) + 6 = 6(7m + 1), a multiple of 6.

methods.name: Factorise directly
methods.summary: 7^n − 1 = (7 − 1)(7^(n − 1) + … + 1) has a factor 6; n³ − n = (n − 1)n(n + 1) is three consecutive integers.

methods.name: Expand (6 + 1)^n
methods.summary: Every term of (6 + 1)^n except the final 1 contains a factor 6, so 7^n − 1 is a multiple of 6.

misconceptions: Writing 7^(k + 1) = 7^k + 7 instead of 7 × 7^k
Showing f(k + 1) − f(k) is a multiple of 6 but never using the hypothesis that f(k) is
Starting the induction at n = 0 when the statement is for n ∈ ℤ+, or omitting the base case

threads.echo: 7^(k + 1) = 7 × 7^k: the inductive step is one more multiplication by the same factor.

skills.name: Prove results about derivatives or inequalities by induction
examTypes: Prove by induction that the nth derivative of x e^x is (x + n)e^x
Prove that d^n/dx^n (e^(2x)) = 2^n e^(2x) for n ∈ ℤ+
Prove that 2^n > n² for all integers n ≥ 5
Find a formula for the nth derivative of 1/x and prove it by induction

methods.name: Differentiate the assumed kth result
methods.summary: Assume the kth derivative is (x + k)e^x; differentiating with the product rule gives e^x + (x + k)e^x = (x + k + 1)e^x.

methods.name: Build a chain of inequalities
methods.summary: Assume 2^k > k²; then 2^(k + 1) = 2 × 2^k > 2k², and 2k² ≥ (k + 1)² when k ≥ 3, which holds since k ≥ 5.

methods.name: Find the pattern first, then prove it
methods.summary: Work out the first few derivatives (−1/x², 2/x³, −6/x⁴) to conjecture (−1)^n n!/x^(n + 1), then prove it by induction.

misconceptions: Using the product rule incorrectly: the derivative of (x + k)e^x given as e^x only, or as (x + k)e^x again
Starting the inequality proof at n = 1, where 2 > 1 holds but n = 2, 3, 4 fail (4 > 4 is false)
For 1/x, losing the alternating sign: claiming the nth derivative is n!/x^(n + 1)

threads.echo: Each inductive step takes one more derivative, so the proof follows the rate of change of the rate of change.

skills.name: Prove a number is irrational by contradiction
examTypes: Prove by contradiction that √5 is irrational
Prove that the cube root of 2 is irrational
Prove that if a is rational and b is irrational, then a − b is irrational
Spot the flaw in a given 'proof' that √4 is irrational

methods.name: Assume p/q in lowest terms and find a common factor
methods.summary: If √5 = p/q in lowest terms, then p² = 5q², so 5 | p; write p = 5m to get q² = 5m², so 5 | q, contradicting lowest terms.

methods.name: Count prime factors
methods.summary: In p² = 5q², the left side has an even number of factors of 5 and the right an odd number, which is impossible.

methods.name: Use closure of the rationals
methods.summary: If a − b = c were rational, then b = a − c would be rational, a contradiction.

misconceptions: Not stating that p/q is in lowest terms, so no contradiction can be reached
Using 'k divides p², so k divides p' for any k: it needs k prime (4 divides 6² = 36 but not 6), which is why the same argument fails for √4 = 2
Proving the statement for one example, such as a = 1 and b = √2, instead of in general

skills.name: Prove general statements by contradiction
examTypes: Prove by contradiction that there are infinitely many prime numbers
Prove that there is no largest even number
Prove that if n² is even then n is even
Prove that there are no positive integers x and y with x² − y² = 2

methods.name: Assume a finite list and build a new number
methods.summary: If p₁, …, pₙ are all the primes, N = p₁p₂…pₙ + 1 leaves remainder 1 on division by each, so N has a prime factor not on the list.

methods.name: Assume the conclusion is false and reach a clash
methods.summary: Suppose n² is even but n is odd, n = 2m + 1; then n² = 4m² + 4m + 1 is odd, a contradiction.

methods.name: Factorise and compare parity
methods.summary: (x − y)(x + y) = 2 with x − y and x + y of the same parity: both odd gives an odd product, both even gives a multiple of 4, so neither can be 2.

misconceptions: Claiming p₁p₂…pₙ + 1 is itself always prime: 2 × 3 × 5 × 7 × 11 × 13 + 1 = 30031 = 59 × 509
Assuming what is to be proved rather than its negation at the start
Stopping at a statement that is merely unlikely rather than a genuine contradiction

skills.name: Disprove a statement with a counterexample and explain why it works
examTypes: Show that 2^p − 1 is not prime for every prime p
Disprove: for all real a and b, √(a² + b²) = a + b
Show that n² − n + 11 is not prime for all n ∈ ℕ
Show that the statement 'there are no positive integers with x² + y² = 25' is false

methods.name: Choose a value that makes the expression factorise
methods.summary: For n² − n + 11, n = 11 gives 11² − 11 + 11 = 121 = 11², which is not prime.

methods.name: Tabulate on the GDC
methods.summary: Generate a table of values to find a candidate, then justify by hand why it fails.

misconceptions: Stating the counterexample without showing why it fails (no factorisation or evaluation)
Giving examples where the statement holds as if they proved it true
Using n = 0 for a statement about n ∈ ℤ+, outside the stated domain

subtopics.title: Systems of linear equations in up to three unknowns
subtopics.guide: Solve systems of up to three linear equations in up to three unknowns, both by algebra (elimination or row reduction) and by technology. Decide whether a system has a unique solution, infinitely many (giving the general solution in terms of a parameter) or none (inconsistent); links to intersecting planes in AHL3.18.

skills.name: Solve a 3 × 3 system with a unique solution by elimination
examTypes: Solve x + y + z = 6, 2x − y + z = 3, x + 2y − z = 2
Use row reduction to solve the system of equations
Show that (1, 2, 3) satisfies all three equations

methods.name: Eliminate one variable to get a 2 × 2 system
methods.summary: Adding the first and third equations removes z: 2x + 3y = 8; the first and second give x − 2y = −3 after subtracting; solve to get x = 1, y = 2, z = 3.

methods.name: Row-reduce the augmented matrix
methods.summary: Write the coefficients and constants in a table and use row operations to reach triangular form, then back-substitute.

methods.name: Substitute from one equation
methods.summary: Make z the subject of one equation and substitute into the other two.

misconceptions: Subtracting the left sides but adding the right sides: x − 2y = 9 instead of −3
Eliminating a different variable from each pair, leaving two equations still in three unknowns
Stopping after finding two unknowns and not back-substituting for the third

threads.echo: The unique solution is the single point where three planes meet; the algebra finds that intersection.

skills.name: Solve a linear system with the GDC
examTypes: Use technology to solve the system 2x + 3y − z = 4.5, x − y + 4z = 1.2, 3x + y + z = 7
Solve a system arising from a costing context and interpret the solution
Use the reduced row-echelon form on the GDC to decide how many solutions the system has

methods.name: Use the simultaneous equations solver
methods.summary: Enter the coefficients row by row; the solver returns x, y and z, or reports no unique solution.

methods.name: Use rref on the augmented matrix
methods.summary: A row of zeros with a non-zero final entry means no solution; a full row of zeros means infinitely many.

methods.name: Use the inverse of the coefficient matrix
methods.summary: If the coefficient matrix is invertible, the solution is its inverse times the constants column.

misconceptions: Entering coefficients in the wrong column when a variable is missing from an equation (not entering 0)
Treating the solver message 'no unique solution' as 'no solution', when there may be infinitely many
Rounding intermediate results too early and getting a solution that fails the original equations

threads.echo: Technology and elimination find the same intersection of planes; use one to check the other.

skills.name: Find parameter values for which a system has a unique solution, infinitely many or none
examTypes: For the system x + y + z = 1, x + 2y + 3z = 2, 2x + 3y + kz = m, find the value of k for which there is no unique solution
Find the value of m for which the system is consistent
Show that the system has no solution and explain what this means
State the conditions on k and m for each type of solution

methods.name: Row-reduce until one equation has a single unknown
methods.summary: Elimination gives y + 2z = 1 and y + (k − 2)z = m − 2, then (k − 4)z = m − 3: unique if k ≠ 4; infinitely many if k = 4 and m = 3; none if k = 4 and m ≠ 3.

methods.name: Set the coefficient determinant to zero
methods.summary: No unique solution exactly when the determinant of the coefficient matrix is 0, which here gives k = 4; then test consistency.

methods.name: Test candidate values on the GDC
methods.summary: Substitute the found k and try rref to see whether the last row is all zeros or 0 = non-zero.

misconceptions: Concluding 'no solution' whenever k = 4 without checking whether m makes the equations consistent
Dividing by (k − 4) without considering k = 4
Reading a final row 0 = 0 as 'no solution' instead of 'infinitely many'

threads.echo: Unique, infinite or none matches three planes meeting at a point, along a line, or with no common point.

skills.name: Write the general solution of a system with infinitely many solutions
examTypes: Find the general solution of x + y + z = 1, x + 2y + 3z = 2, 2x + 3y + 4z = 3
Express x and y in terms of z = λ
Verify that your general solution satisfies all three equations
Interpret the general solution geometrically

methods.name: Set the free variable to λ and back-substitute
methods.summary: Reduction gives y + 2z = 1; put z = λ, so y = 1 − 2λ and x = 1 − y − z = λ.

methods.name: Write the solution as a line
methods.summary: (x, y, z) = (0, 1, 0) + λ(1, −2, 1): the three planes share this line (AHL3.18).

methods.name: Read the dependence from rref
methods.summary: The rref rows x − z = 0 and y + 2z = 1 give the same general solution.

misconceptions: Giving one particular solution, such as (0, 1, 0), as the whole answer
Introducing two parameters when only one variable is free
Making an arithmetic slip in back-substitution so the answer fails the third equation (e.g. x = 2λ)

threads.echo: The general solution is a point plus λ times a direction vector: the line where the planes meet.
Infinitely many algebraic solutions correspond to a whole line of intersection rather than a single point.

skills.name: Set up a linear system from a context and solve it
examTypes: The curve y = ax² + bx + c passes through (1, 2), (2, 7) and (−1, 4); find a, b and c
Three items cost given totals in three different combinations; find the price of each
A total of 50 tickets of three types were sold; form and solve a system from the given information

methods.name: Substitute each condition to get one equation
methods.summary: a + b + c = 2, 4a + 2b + c = 7, a − b + c = 4; subtracting the first and third gives b = −1, then a = 2 and c = 1, so y = 2x² − x + 1.

methods.name: Solve the system on the GDC
methods.summary: Once the equations are written, use the simultaneous solver or rref on Paper 2.

methods.name: Check the answer makes sense
methods.summary: Substitute back and check the values are sensible in context, such as whole numbers of tickets.

misconceptions: Substituting (−1, 4) as a − b + c = −4 or as −a − b + c = 4
Defining variables inconsistently between equations in a word problem
Accepting a non-integer number of tickets without questioning it

threads.echo: Three points determine a parabola: solving the system is the algebraic way to find the graph that passes through all three.

subtopics.title: Polynomial functions: factor and remainder theorems, sum and product of roots
subtopics.guide: Polynomial functions of any degree: their graphs, zeros, roots and factors; the factor and remainder theorems; and the sum (−aₙ₋₁/aₙ) and product ((−1)ⁿa₀/aₙ) of the roots of a polynomial equation, including equations with complex roots. Only the sum and the product of the roots are listed, not sums of pairwise products.

skills.name: Find a remainder with the remainder theorem
examTypes: Find the remainder when P(x) is divided by (x − 2)
Find the remainder when P(x) is divided by (2x − 1)
P(x) leaves remainder 5 when divided by (x + 1); find the value of the constant k

methods.name: Evaluate P at the root of the divisor
methods.summary: The remainder on dividing by (x − a) is P(a); for (ax − b) it is P(b/a). For P(x) = x³ − 2x² + 5x − 3 and (x − 2): P(2) = 8 − 8 + 10 − 3 = 7.

methods.name: Polynomial long division
methods.summary: Divide P(x) by the linear factor term by term; the constant left at the end is the remainder.

methods.name: Synthetic division
methods.summary: Run the coefficients through synthetic division with the root of the divisor; the last number in the bottom row is the remainder.

misconceptions: Evaluates P(−2) instead of P(2) for the divisor (x − 2), giving −29 instead of 7 for x³ − 2x² + 5x − 3
For the divisor (2x − 1) evaluates P(1) or P(2) instead of P(1/2), e.g. 1 instead of −7/8 for x³ − 2x² + 5x − 3
Thinks the remainder on dividing by (2x − 1) is 2 × P(1/2)

threads.echo: P(x) = (x − a)Q(x) + R is the same polynomial rewritten so that putting x = a wipes out everything except the remainder.

skills.name: Use the factor theorem to test factors and find unknown coefficients
examTypes: Show that (x + 3) is a factor of P(x)
Given that (x − 1) is a factor of P(x), find the value of a
(x − 2) is a factor of P(x) and the remainder on division by (x + 1) is −6; find a and b

methods.name: Set P(a) = 0 and solve
methods.summary: A factor (x − a) means P(a) = 0; each factor or remainder condition gives one linear equation in the unknown coefficients, then solve simultaneously.

methods.name: Divide and force a zero remainder
methods.summary: Carry out the division with the unknown coefficients and set the remainder expression equal to 0.

methods.name: Write P(x) = (x − a)(quadratic) and compare
methods.summary: Write the polynomial as the factor times a general quadratic and match coefficients of each power of x.

misconceptions: Uses P(−3) = 0 when told (x − 3) is a factor
Sets P(a) equal to a (or to 1) instead of 0 for the factor condition
Mixes up the two conditions and sets the remainder condition equal to 0 as well

threads.echo: (x − a) is a factor exactly when the graph of y = P(x) crosses or touches the x-axis at x = a, so an algebraic test and a graph feature are the same fact.

skills.name: Factorise a cubic or quartic fully and solve P(x) = 0
examTypes: Factorise x³ − 6x² + 11x − 6 completely
Hence solve P(x) = 0
Given that x = 1/2 is a root, find the other roots of 2x³ + … = 0

methods.name: Find one root by trial, then divide
methods.summary: Test candidates ±(factors of a₀)/(factors of aₙ) until P(a) = 0, divide by (x − a) and factorise or solve the quadratic quotient.

methods.name: Write the quotient by inspection
methods.summary: With one factor known, write P(x) = (x − a)(px² + qx + r), reading p from the leading term and r from the constant, then find q from one middle coefficient.

methods.name: Polynomial root finder or graph
methods.summary: On Paper 2, use the GDC polynomial solver or the x-intercepts of the graph to find the roots, then write the factors.

misconceptions: Writes the roots of (x − 1)(x − 2)(x − 3) = 0 as −1, −2, −3
Tests only integer candidates when the leading coefficient is not 1, so misses a root such as x = 1/2
Stops after finding one factor and leaves the quadratic quotient unfactorised

threads.echo: Expanded form shows the y-intercept and end behaviour; factorised form shows every root at once.
Each root of P(x) = 0 is an x-intercept of y = P(x), so a sketch or GDC graph suggests which value to try first.

skills.name: Sketch a polynomial from its factors, or find the polynomial from its graph
examTypes: Sketch y = (x + 1)²(x − 2), showing the intercepts
The graph of a cubic touches the x-axis at x = −1, crosses at x = 2 and passes through (0, 4); find its equation
Which graph shows y = −x(x − 3)²?

methods.name: Roots, multiplicity and end behaviour
methods.summary: Mark the roots, cross at single roots, touch at double roots, flatten through triple roots, and use the sign and degree of the leading term for the ends.

methods.name: Write y = a(x − p)ᵐ(x − q)ⁿ and use one point
methods.summary: Build the factors from the intercepts and their multiplicities, then substitute a known point to find a: for (0, 4), a(1)(−2) = 4 gives a = −2.

methods.name: Graph on the GDC and compare
methods.summary: Graph the candidate polynomial and check intercepts, touching points and end behaviour against the given sketch.

misconceptions: Draws the curve crossing the axis at a double root instead of touching it
Forgets the leading constant a, so y = (x + 1)²(x − 2) gives y-intercept −2 instead of the required 4
Gets the end behaviour wrong when the leading coefficient is negative, e.g. draws y = −x(x − 3)² rising to the right

threads.echo: The factorised equation and the sketch carry the same information: each factor is an intercept and each power is a crossing or touching pattern.

skills.name: Use the sum and product of the roots of a polynomial equation
examTypes: Write down the sum and the product of the roots of 2x³ − 5x² + 3x + 7 = 0
The roots of a cubic are α, 2α and 3α; use the sum of the roots to find α
A cubic with real coefficients has roots 2 and 1 + i; find the product of its roots and hence a coefficient

methods.name: Sum = −aₙ₋₁/aₙ, product = (−1)ⁿa₀/aₙ
methods.summary: Read the two coefficients and the degree: for 2x³ − 5x² + 3x + 7 = 0 the sum is 5/2 and the product is (−1)³ × 7/2 = −7/2.

methods.name: Expand aₙ(x − α)(x − β)(x − γ) and compare
methods.summary: Expanding the factorised form shows the x² coefficient is −aₙ(α + β + γ) and the constant is −aₙαβγ, which is where the formulas come from.

methods.name: Pair complex conjugate roots
methods.summary: With real coefficients, a root 1 + i brings 1 − i, whose sum 2 and product 2 are real, so the sum and product of all roots stay real.

misconceptions: Drops the minus sign and gives the sum of the roots of 2x³ − 5x² + 3x + 7 = 0 as −5/2
Ignores (−1)ⁿ and gives the product of the roots of the cubic as 7/2 instead of −7/2
Forgets to divide by the leading coefficient and gives the sum as 5
Uses the formula with the coefficients listed from the constant upwards, so the sum becomes −3/7

threads.echo: The expanded and factorised forms of the same polynomial must agree, so the coefficients secretly record the sum and the product of the roots.
Complex roots of a real polynomial come in mirror-image pairs across the real axis, which is why their sum and product are real.

subtopics.title: Rational functions with a quadratic numerator or denominator
subtopics.guide: Rational functions with a linear numerator over a quadratic denominator, and with a quadratic numerator over a linear denominator, with the reciprocal function as a special case. Sketches must show every asymptote (vertical, horizontal and oblique) and all axis intercepts.

skills.name: Find the vertical asymptotes of a rational function with a quadratic denominator
examTypes: Write down the equations of the vertical asymptotes of f(x) = (2x + 1)/(x² − x − 6)
Explain why the graph of y = (x + 1)/(x² + 4) has no vertical asymptote
The graph of f has vertical asymptotes x = 1 and x = −3; find the constants in the denominator

methods.name: Factorise the denominator and set each factor to zero
methods.summary: x² − x − 6 = (x − 3)(x + 2), so the vertical asymptotes are x = 3 and x = −2 (as long as the numerator is not also zero there).

methods.name: Count asymptotes with the discriminant
methods.summary: The quadratic denominator has two, one or no real zeros as b² − 4ac is positive, zero or negative, so the graph has two, one or no vertical asymptotes.

methods.name: Graph or table on the GDC
methods.summary: Graph the function or tabulate values close to a suspected asymptote to see the output grow without bound.

misconceptions: Sets the numerator equal to zero and gives x = −1/2 as a vertical asymptote of (2x + 1)/(x² − x − 6)
Factorises x² − x − 6 as (x + 3)(x − 2) and gives the asymptotes as x = −3 and x = 2
Thinks every quadratic denominator gives two vertical asymptotes, even x² + 4

threads.echo: The zeros of the denominator, found by algebra, are exactly the vertical lines the graph runs up against.

skills.name: Find the horizontal asymptote of (ax + b)/(cx² + dx + e) and where the curve crosses it
examTypes: Write down the equation of the horizontal asymptote of f(x) = (2x + 1)/(x² − x − 6)
Find the coordinates of the point where the graph crosses its horizontal asymptote
Describe the behaviour of f(x) as x → ∞ and as x → −∞

methods.name: Compare degrees
methods.summary: The denominator has the higher degree, so f(x) → 0 for large |x| and the horizontal asymptote is y = 0.

methods.name: Divide top and bottom by x²
methods.summary: (2/x + 1/x²)/(1 − 1/x − 6/x²) tends to 0/1 = 0 as |x| grows.

methods.name: Solve f(x) = 0 for the crossing point
methods.summary: The curve meets y = 0 where the numerator is zero: 2x + 1 = 0 gives the crossing (−1/2, 0).

methods.name: Tabulate large x on the GDC
methods.summary: Values at x = ±100, ±1000 shrink towards 0, confirming the asymptote and which side the curve approaches from.

misconceptions: Gives the horizontal asymptote as y = 2 by taking the ratio of the leading coefficients regardless of degree
Believes a graph can never cross its horizontal asymptote, so misses the crossing at (−1/2, 0)
Gives the horizontal asymptote as y = b/e (the ratio of the constants), i.e. y = −1/6

threads.echo: The horizontal asymptote describes the far ends of the graph, but solving f(x) = 0 shows the middle of the graph can still cross it.

skills.name: Find the oblique asymptote of (ax² + bx + c)/(dx + e)
examTypes: Express (x² + 3x + 5)/(x + 1) in the form px + q + r/(x + 1)
Hence write down the equations of all the asymptotes of the graph
Find the values of the constants given that the graph has oblique asymptote y = 2x − 1

methods.name: Divide the numerator by the denominator
methods.summary: (x² + 3x + 5) ÷ (x + 1) = x + 2 remainder 3, so f(x) = x + 2 + 3/(x + 1) and the oblique asymptote is y = x + 2.

methods.name: Write (px + q)(x + 1) + r and compare
methods.summary: Expand (px + q)(x + 1) + r and match it with x² + 3x + 5: p = 1, p + q = 3, q + r = 5.

methods.name: Remainder term vanishes for large x
methods.summary: As |x| grows, r/(dx + e) → 0, so the graph approaches the straight line px + q; a GDC graph of both confirms it.

misconceptions: Takes only the leading terms and gives the oblique asymptote of (x² + 3x + 5)/(x + 1) as y = x
Divides each numerator term by x and gives y = x + 3
Gives a horizontal asymptote y = 1 as well as the oblique one, by taking the ratio of leading coefficients

threads.echo: x + 2 + 3/(x + 1) is the same function as (x² + 3x + 5)/(x + 1), rewritten so that the asymptote line and the vertical asymptote can be read off.

skills.name: Find the range and turning points of a rational function
examTypes: Find the range of f(x) = x/(x² + 1)
Find the set of values of y that the graph of y = (x² + 3x + 5)/(x + 1) never takes
Find the coordinates of the local maximum and minimum points of f

methods.name: Rearrange y = f(x) into a quadratic in x
methods.summary: From y = x/(x² + 1), yx² − x + y = 0 has real x only when 1 − 4y² ≥ 0, so −1/2 ≤ y ≤ 1/2.

methods.name: Differentiate and find stationary points
methods.summary: Use the quotient rule (or differentiate x + 2 + 3/(x + 1)) and solve f′(x) = 0; the turning values bound the range.

methods.name: GDC maximum and minimum
methods.summary: Graph f and use the max/min tools to find the turning values, together with the asymptotes, to state the range.

misconceptions: States the range as all real numbers except the horizontal asymptote value, e.g. y ≠ 0 for x/(x² + 1)
Takes the wrong side of the discriminant condition and gives the gap 1 − 2√3 < y < 1 + 2√3 as the range of (x² + 3x + 5)/(x + 1), instead of y ≤ 1 − 2√3 or y ≥ 1 + 2√3
Assumes the local maximum is above the local minimum, so rejects correct turning values on separate branches

threads.echo: The extreme values of a rational function come from f′(x) = 0 or from the discriminant of a quadratic hitting zero: the same tangency idea as a line just touching a curve.
Asking which y-values are possible is asking which horizontal lines meet the graph, and the discriminant counts those meetings.

skills.name: Sketch a rational function with all its asymptotes and intercepts
examTypes: Sketch the graph of y = (2x + 1)/(x² − x − 6), showing all asymptotes and axis intercepts
Sketch y = (x² + 3x + 5)/(x + 1), labelling the oblique asymptote
Which graph shows y = (x − 1)/(x² − 4)?

methods.name: Asymptotes, intercepts, then a sign check
methods.summary: Draw every asymptote, mark the x- and y-intercepts, and test the sign of f in each interval between the zeros and asymptotes to place each branch.

methods.name: Graph on the GDC and transfer
methods.summary: Graph f with a suitable window, read the intercepts and asymptotes, and copy the shape, taking care near each asymptote.

methods.name: Build from the denominator's graph
methods.summary: For a constant or slowly changing numerator, think of 1/(quadratic): zeros of the quadratic become vertical asymptotes and its vertex becomes a turning point.

misconceptions: Draws the middle branch of (2x + 1)/(x² − x − 6) without crossing the x-axis at x = −1/2
Gives the y-intercept as the ratio of leading coefficients instead of f(0), e.g. 2 instead of −1/6
Draws the curve crossing a vertical asymptote

threads.echo: Each algebraic fact (zeros of top and bottom, the degree comparison, the sign in each interval) fixes one feature of the sketch.

subtopics.title: Odd and even functions, inverses with a restricted domain, self-inverse functions
subtopics.guide: Odd functions (f(−x) = −f(x)) and even functions (f(−x) = f(x)), including periodic ones such as sin, cos and tan; finding an inverse function, restricting the domain where needed so that one exists; and self-inverse functions, where f⁻¹ = f.

skills.name: Decide algebraically whether a function is odd, even or neither
examTypes: Show that f(x) = x³ − x is an odd function
Determine whether g(x) = x sin x is odd, even or neither
Prove that h(x) = x² + x is neither odd nor even

methods.name: Simplify f(−x) and compare
methods.summary: Replace x by −x, simplify, and compare with f(x) and −f(x): (−x)³ − (−x) = −(x³ − x), so x³ − x is odd.

methods.name: One counterexample for 'neither'
methods.summary: To show a function is neither, find one value with f(−a) ≠ f(a) and one with f(−a) ≠ −f(a): h(1) = 2, h(−1) = 0.

methods.name: Use known odd and even pieces
methods.summary: Odd powers, sin and tan are odd; even powers, constants and cos are even; combine them using the product and sum rules.

misconceptions: Concludes a function is odd just because f(−x) ≠ f(x)
Calls f(x) = x³ + 1 odd because the power is odd, though f(−x) = −x³ + 1 ≠ −f(x)
Checks one value such as f(−1) = f(1) and concludes the function is even
Believes every function must be either odd or even

threads.echo: f(−x) = f(x) is mirror symmetry in the y-axis and f(−x) = −f(x) is half-turn symmetry about the origin, so half the graph gives the other half free.

skills.name: Recognise and complete graphs of odd and even functions
examTypes: The graph of f is shown for x ≥ 0; complete it for x < 0 given that f is odd
Which of these graphs shows an even function?
State whether sin x, cos x and tan x are odd or even, and explain from their graphs

methods.name: Reflect in the y-axis or rotate about the origin
methods.summary: For an even function reflect the known half in the y-axis; for an odd function rotate it by 180° about the origin (reflect in both axes).

methods.name: Map key points
methods.summary: Send each key point (a, b) to (−a, b) for even or (−a, −b) for odd, then join them in the same shape.

methods.name: Use the unit circle for trig functions
methods.summary: The angle −θ is the reflection of θ in the x-axis, so cos(−θ) = cos θ and sin(−θ) = −sin θ.

misconceptions: Completes an odd function by reflecting only in the y-axis, which produces an even function
Completes an odd function by reflecting only in the x-axis
Draws an odd function that is defined at 0 but does not pass through the origin

threads.echo: Even and odd are the symmetry of y = x² and y = x³; the same symmetry gives sin(−x) = −sin x and cos(−x) = cos x.
A function is even when reflecting in the y-axis, f(−x), leaves the graph unchanged, and odd when that reflection equals reflecting in the x-axis.

skills.name: Combine odd and even functions and use the results
examTypes: Prove that the product of two odd functions is even
Given that f is odd and g is even, determine whether f ∘ g and f × g are odd or even
Hence write down the value of ∫ from −2 to 2 of x³ cos x dx

methods.name: Prove from the definitions
methods.summary: For odd f and g, (fg)(−x) = f(−x)g(−x) = (−f(x))(−g(x)) = f(x)g(x), so fg is even.

methods.name: Treat odd as −1 and even as +1 under multiplication
methods.summary: Odd × odd and even × even are even; odd × even is odd, like multiplying signs.

methods.name: Cancel areas for an odd integrand
methods.summary: An odd function's area on [−a, 0] is the negative of its area on [0, a], so its integral from −a to a is 0.

misconceptions: Thinks the product of two odd functions is odd
Assumes the sum of an odd and an even function is odd or even, e.g. calls x³ + x² odd
Uses ∫ from −a to a of f(x) dx = 0 for an even function

threads.echo: Knowing that x³ cos x is odd gives its integral over [−2, 2] as 0 without any integration.
An odd function's signed area on one side of the y-axis cancels its area on the other, so symmetric pieces add to zero.

skills.name: Restrict a domain so an inverse exists, then find f⁻¹ with its domain
examTypes: Find the largest value of a such that f(x) = x² − 4x + 1, x ≤ a, has an inverse
For f(x) = x² − 4x + 1, x ≥ 2, find f⁻¹(x) and state its domain
Explain why f does not have an inverse on its full domain

methods.name: Complete the square, then rearrange
methods.summary: x² − 4x + 1 = (x − 2)² − 3; swap and solve: y = 2 + √(x + 3), taking the + root because the domain is x ≥ 2; domain of f⁻¹ is x ≥ −3.

methods.name: Restrict at the turning point
methods.summary: Solve f′(x) = 0 to find where f stops being one-to-one; the largest domain is on one side of that x-value.

methods.name: Horizontal line test
methods.summary: Sketch f: if a horizontal line meets the graph twice, cut the domain at the vertex so each output comes from one input.

methods.name: Solve x = f(y) with the quadratic formula
methods.summary: Treat y² − 4y + (1 − x) = 0 as a quadratic in y and choose the sign that matches the restricted domain.

misconceptions: Leaves f⁻¹(x) = 2 ± √(x + 3), not choosing the branch
Chooses 2 − √(x + 3) when the restricted domain is x ≥ 2
Gives the domain of f⁻¹ as x ≥ 2 (the domain of f) instead of x ≥ −3 (the range of f)

threads.echo: x² has an undo only after cutting it down to one side of its vertex, which is the same reason arcsin returns only one angle.

skills.name: Show that a function is self-inverse, or find a constant that makes it so
examTypes: Show that f(x) = (3x + 1)/(x − 3) is self-inverse
Find the value of k for which f(x) = (kx + 2)/(x − 4) is self-inverse
Show that f(x) = √(4 − x²), 0 ≤ x ≤ 2, is its own inverse

methods.name: Show f(f(x)) = x
methods.summary: Substitute f into itself and simplify: for (3x + 1)/(x − 3) the compound fraction reduces to 10x/10 = x.

methods.name: Find f⁻¹ and compare with f
methods.summary: Swap x and y, rearrange, and check the result is the original formula on the same domain.

methods.name: Graph symmetric in y = x
methods.summary: A self-inverse graph is its own reflection in y = x; for (ax + b)/(cx + d) this happens when d = −a, so k = 4.

misconceptions: Thinks self-inverse means f(x) × f(x) = 1 or f(x) = 1/f(x)
Checks f(f(a)) = a for one value only and concludes the function is self-inverse
Confuses self-inverse with odd, and claims f(x) = x³ is self-inverse

threads.echo: A self-inverse process undoes itself, like 1/x or 5 − x: doing it twice gets you back where you started.
f = f⁻¹ means the graph is unchanged by reflection in y = x.

skills.name: Find where the graphs of f and f⁻¹ intersect
examTypes: Sketch y = f(x) and y = f⁻¹(x) on the same axes
Solve f(x) = f⁻¹(x) for f(x) = (x² + 6)/5, x ≥ 0
Explain why the intersection points of an increasing function and its inverse lie on y = x

methods.name: Solve f(x) = x for an increasing f
methods.summary: For increasing f, f and f⁻¹ meet only on y = x: (x² + 6)/5 = x gives x = 2 or 3, so (2, 2) and (3, 3).

methods.name: Find f⁻¹ and solve f(x) = f⁻¹(x)
methods.summary: Write f⁻¹ explicitly and solve the equation directly; needed when f is decreasing.

methods.name: Graph both on the GDC
methods.summary: Graph f, f⁻¹ and y = x and use the intersect tool to find every meeting point.

misconceptions: Solves f(x) = x for the decreasing function f(x) = −x³ and finds only (0, 0), missing (1, −1) and (−1, 1)
Reflects the graph in the y-axis instead of y = x to draw f⁻¹
Gives f⁻¹(x) = 1/f(x) and solves f(x) = 1/f(x)

threads.echo: f⁻¹ is f reflected in y = x, so points where the curve meets the mirror line are shared by both.
Solving f(x) = f⁻¹(x) is finding intersections, and the graph shows whether the shortcut f(x) = x is safe.

subtopics.title: Solving inequalities g(x) ≥ f(x) graphically and analytically
subtopics.guide: Solving inequalities of the form g(x) ≥ f(x) both from graphs and analytically. Algebraic or graphical methods are expected for simple polynomials up to degree 3; technology is used for these and for other functions.

skills.name: Solve a polynomial inequality up to degree 3 algebraically
examTypes: Solve x³ ≥ 4x
Solve x³ − 2x² − 5x + 6 < 0, given that (x − 1) is a factor
Find the set of values of x for which (x + 2)(x − 1)² > 0

methods.name: Rearrange to h(x) ≥ 0, factorise, use a sign diagram
methods.summary: x³ − 4x = x(x − 2)(x + 2) ≥ 0; test the sign in each interval between −2, 0 and 2, giving −2 ≤ x ≤ 0 or x ≥ 2.

methods.name: Sketch the factorised cubic
methods.summary: Sketch y = x(x − 2)(x + 2) using its roots and end behaviour, and read where the curve is on or above the x-axis.

methods.name: Check on the GDC
methods.summary: Graph both sides and confirm the intervals between the intersection points.

misconceptions: Divides both sides of x³ ≥ 4x by x and gives x ≤ −2 or x ≥ 2, losing −2 ≤ x ≤ 0
Gives only x ≥ 2 after taking the positive square root of x² ≥ 4
Uses the sign pattern of a positive cubic for a cubic with a negative leading coefficient
Treats the double root x = 1 as a sign change and gives x > 1 for (x + 2)(x − 1)² > 0, instead of x > −2, x ≠ 1

threads.echo: The sign diagram is the graph of x³ − 4x squeezed onto a number line: it says above or below the axis in each interval.

skills.name: Solve g(x) ≥ f(x) from given graphs
examTypes: Use the graphs of f and g to solve g(x) ≥ f(x)
The graphs intersect at x = −1 and x = 3; write down the solution of f(x) < g(x)
Which interval satisfies the inequality shown by the shaded region?

methods.name: Find where g is above f between intersections
methods.summary: Mark the x-coordinates of the intersections, then pick the intervals where the graph of g lies on or above the graph of f.

methods.name: Think of g − f against the x-axis
methods.summary: g(x) ≥ f(x) is the same as g(x) − f(x) ≥ 0, so look for where the difference graph is above the axis.

misconceptions: Reads where g(x) ≥ 0 instead of where g(x) ≥ f(x)
Gives the answer as y-values instead of x-values
Gives the complementary interval, e.g. −1 < x < 3 instead of x < −1 or x > 3

threads.echo: An inequality is an intersection question with a direction: find where the graphs meet, then which one is on top.

skills.name: Solve an inequality involving other functions with technology
examTypes: Solve eˣ > x + 2
Solve ln x ≥ x − 2, giving the end points to three significant figures
Solve sin x < x/3 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π

methods.name: Graph both sides and intersect
methods.summary: Graph y = eˣ and y = x + 2, find the intersections x ≈ −1.84 and x ≈ 1.15, and read off x < −1.84 or x > 1.15.

methods.name: Zeros of the difference
methods.summary: Graph y = eˣ − x − 2, find its zeros and read where the graph is above the x-axis.

methods.name: Check the domain and asymptotes
methods.summary: Exclude values outside the domain (for example x ≤ 0 for ln x) and any vertical asymptotes before stating the intervals.

misconceptions: Gives the interval between the intersections, −1.84 < x < 1.15, for eˣ > x + 2
Uses a window too small to show a second intersection, and gives only one boundary
Ignores the domain and includes x ≤ 0 in the solution of an inequality with ln x

threads.echo: eˣ = x + 2 has no algebraic solution, so the graph or GDC is the method, not just a check.

skills.name: Solve an inequality with a variable in the denominator
examTypes: Solve 1/(x − 1) < x + 1
Explain why multiplying both sides by (x − 2) is not valid

methods.name: Graph both sides on the GDC
methods.summary: Graph y = (x + 1)/(x − 2) and y = 3, find the intersection x = 3.5 and use the asymptote x = 2 as a second boundary: 2 < x ≤ 3.5.

methods.name: Combine into one fraction and use a sign diagram
methods.summary: (x + 1)/(x − 2) − 3 = (7 − 2x)/(x − 2) ≥ 0; the critical values are 2 and 3.5, and x = 2 is excluded.

methods.name: Multiply by the square of the denominator
methods.summary: Multiply both sides by (x − 2)², which is positive, to get (x + 1)(x − 2) ≥ 3(x − 2)², then solve the quadratic inequality and exclude x = 2.

misconceptions: Multiplies both sides of (x + 1)/(x − 2) ≥ 3 by (x − 2) and gives x ≤ 3.5, which includes values below 2
Includes x = 2 in the answer, writing 2 ≤ x ≤ 3.5
Gives only the intersection x = 3.5 as the boundary and misses the asymptote

threads.echo: The graph shows the asymptote as a second boundary that the algebra hides when you multiply through carelessly.

skills.name: Use an inequality to compare two models in context
examTypes: Find the times for which the population of town A exceeds that of town B
For what range of production levels is the revenue at least the cost?
Find the interval of time for which the first tank holds more water than the second

methods.name: Graph both models and intersect
methods.summary: Graph both models over the context domain, find the intersections and read the interval where the required model is on top.

methods.name: Rearrange and factorise if the models are polynomial
methods.summary: Write the difference of the two models as one polynomial, factorise and use a sign diagram, keeping only values allowed by the context.

methods.name: Restrict to the meaningful domain
methods.summary: Discard negative times or quantities and round the boundaries in the direction the context demands.

misconceptions: Includes negative times in the answer because the algebra allows them
Rounds a boundary the wrong way, e.g. gives 'at least 12 items' when the break-even point is 12.4
Gives the value of the models at the intersection instead of the time

threads.echo: Which model is bigger, and when, is the same intersection-plus-direction question, now with the context limiting the domain.

subtopics.title: Graphs of |f(x)|, f(|x|), 1/f(x), f(ax + b) and [f(x)]²; modulus equations and inequalities
subtopics.guide: Graphs of y = |f(x)|, y = f(|x|), y = 1/f(x), y = f(ax + b) and y = [f(x)]² drawn from the graph of y = f(x); and solving equations and inequalities that involve the modulus, algebraically for simple cases and with technology otherwise.

skills.name: Sketch y = |f(x)| and y = f(|x|) from the graph of y = f(x)
examTypes: Sketch y = |x² − 2x − 3|, showing the intercepts and the image of the vertex
Sketch y = f(|x|) for the function shown
Which graph shows y = |f(x)| and which shows y = f(|x|)?

methods.name: |f(x)|: reflect the part below the axis
methods.summary: Keep the graph where f(x) ≥ 0 and reflect the rest in the x-axis: the vertex (1, −4) of x² − 2x − 3 becomes (1, 4).

methods.name: f(|x|): keep x ≥ 0 and reflect it in the y-axis
methods.summary: Delete the graph for x < 0 and replace it with the mirror image of the x ≥ 0 part, so f(|x|) is always even.

methods.name: Write as a piecewise function
methods.summary: |f(x)| is f(x) where f(x) ≥ 0 and −f(x) where f(x) < 0; f(|x|) is f(x) for x ≥ 0 and f(−x) for x < 0.

misconceptions: Swaps the two: reflects the x < 0 part for |f(x)| or the negative part for f(|x|)
Keeps the left-hand x-intercept −1 when sketching f(|x|) for f(x) = x² − 2x − 3, whose correct intercepts are ±3
Reflects the whole graph of f in the x-axis for |f(x)|

threads.echo: |f(x)| works on outputs and f(|x|) works on inputs, just as adding outside the function moves vertically and inside moves horizontally.
f(|x|) is always an even function: the graph for x ≥ 0 decides the whole picture.

skills.name: Sketch y = 1/f(x) from the graph of y = f(x)
examTypes: Sketch y = 1/(x² − 4), showing its asymptotes and turning point
The graph of f has a minimum at (0, −4) and zeros at ±2; sketch y = 1/f(x)
Which feature of y = f(x) becomes a vertical asymptote of y = 1/f(x)?

methods.name: Swap features point by point
methods.summary: Zeros of f become vertical asymptotes, vertical asymptotes become zeros, a maximum (a, k) becomes a minimum (a, 1/k), and points where f = ±1 stay fixed.

methods.name: Same sign, opposite size
methods.summary: 1/f has the same sign as f; where |f| is large, 1/f is near 0, and where f is near 0, 1/f is large.

methods.name: Graph on the GDC and compare
methods.summary: Graph f and 1/f together to check the asymptotes and the turning points line up.

misconceptions: Maps the minimum (0, −4) of x² − 4 to (0, 4) or (0, −4) instead of the maximum (0, −1/4)
Confuses 1/f(x) with f⁻¹(x) and reflects the graph in y = x
Draws 1/f with the opposite sign to f in some interval

threads.echo: 1/f(x) is the multiplicative reciprocal, not the inverse function f⁻¹; mixing them up is the same slip as reading sin⁻¹x as 1/sin x.
Where f is largest, 1/f is smallest: a maximum of f at (a, k) becomes a minimum of 1/f at (a, 1/k).

skills.name: Sketch y = f(ax + b) and find the image of a point
examTypes: Describe a sequence of transformations that maps y = f(x) onto y = f(2x + 6)
The point (4, 1) lies on y = f(x); find its image on y = f(2x + 6)
Sketch y = f(3 − x) from the graph of f

methods.name: Translate by (−b, 0), then stretch by 1/a
methods.summary: f(x) → f(x + 6) → f(2x + 6): translate by (−6, 0), then stretch horizontally by scale factor 1/2.

methods.name: Factor out a: f(a(x + b/a))
methods.summary: f(2x + 6) = f(2(x + 3)): stretch by 1/2 first, then translate by (−3, 0).

methods.name: Solve ax + b = p for an image point
methods.summary: The point (p, q) moves to the x that makes the input equal p: 2x + 6 = 4 gives (−1, 1).

misconceptions: Stretches first and then translates by (−6, 0), sending (4, 1) to (−4, 1) instead of (−1, 1)
Stretches horizontally by scale factor 2 instead of 1/2 for f(2x)
Translates by (6, 0) because of the + 6

threads.echo: Changes inside the bracket act on x in reverse: subtract b first, then divide by a, so the order of the moves matters.
The translation part of f(2(x + 3)) is the vector (−3, 0), applied after the stretch.

skills.name: Sketch y = [f(x)]² from the graph of y = f(x)
examTypes: Sketch y = [f(x)]² for the function shown, labelling any points where it touches the x-axis
Sketch y = sin²x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π and state its period
Explain why every zero of f is a minimum point of [f(x)]²

methods.name: Square each output
methods.summary: All outputs become non-negative; zeros of f become points where the graph touches the axis; values with |f| < 1 shrink and |f| > 1 grow; points with f = ±1 go to height 1.

methods.name: Use d/dx [f(x)]² = 2f(x)f′(x)
methods.summary: Stationary points of f² are the stationary points of f plus the zeros of f, which shows each zero becomes a minimum.

methods.name: Graph on the GDC
methods.summary: Graph f and f² together to check the touching points and the heights of turning points.

misconceptions: Draws [f(x)]² crossing the x-axis at the zeros of f instead of touching it
Treats [f(x)]² like |f(x)|, keeping the heights of the reflected parts unchanged, e.g. a minimum of −3 becomes 3 instead of 9
Gives the period of sin²x as 2π instead of π

threads.echo: Squaring turns every zero of f into a minimum and every turning point of f into a turning point of f², because 2f f′ = 0 at both.
Like |f(x)|, squaring acts on outputs only, so x-coordinates of zeros and turning points stay where they were.

skills.name: Solve equations involving the modulus
examTypes: Solve |2x − 1| = |x + 3|
Solve |x − 2| = 2x + 1
Find the number of solutions of |x² − 4| = k for different values of k

methods.name: Square both sides
methods.summary: When both sides are moduli, square: (2x − 1)² = (x + 3)² gives 3x² − 10x − 8 = 0, so x = 4 or x = −2/3.

methods.name: Split into cases and check
methods.summary: Solve x − 2 = 2x + 1 and −(x − 2) = 2x + 1, then reject any solution that makes the right-hand side negative: x = 1/3 only.

methods.name: Intersect the graphs
methods.summary: Sketch both sides (the modulus graph has a V or reflected shape) and count or find the intersections, using the GDC on Paper 2.
