misconceptions: Keeps x = −3 as a solution of |x − 2| = 2x + 1, though the right-hand side is then −5
Solves only 2x − 1 = x + 3 and misses x = −2/3
Squares |x − 2| = 2x + 1 and keeps both roots without checking

threads.echo: A V-shaped graph meets a line at most twice, so the sketch tells you how many of the algebraic cases survive.

skills.name: Solve inequalities involving the modulus
examTypes: Solve |x − 3| < 2
Solve |x + 1| ≥ 2|x − 1|
Solve |3x arccos x| > 1 using technology

methods.name: Read |x − a| < b as a distance
methods.summary: |x − 3| < 2 means x is less than 2 from 3, so 1 < x < 5.

methods.name: Square both sides and solve a quadratic inequality
Graph both sides on the GDC
methods.summary: For harder cases, graph each side, find the intersections and read where the modulus graph is above or below, respecting the domain (−1 ≤ x ≤ 1 for arccos).

misconceptions: Solves |x − 3| < 2 as x < 5 only, ignoring the lower bound
Writes |x − 3| > 2 as the impossible chain −2 > x − 3 > 2 instead of x < 1 or x > 5
Ignores the domain of arccos and gives solutions outside −1 ≤ x ≤ 1

threads.echo: Squaring, splitting into cases and reading the graph are three routes to the same intervals; the graph shows why the answer is one interval or two.
|x − 3| < 2 is an interval symmetric about 3, the centre the modulus measures distance from.

subtopics.title: Reciprocal trigonometric ratios, Pythagorean identities and inverse trigonometric functions
subtopics.guide: Defines sec θ, cosec θ and cot θ as the reciprocals of cos θ, sin θ and tan θ, and adds the Pythagorean identities 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ and 1 + cot²θ = cosec²θ. Covers arcsin x, arccos x and arctan x as functions: their restricted domains, principal-value ranges and graphs.

skills.name: Find exact values of sec, cosec and cot
examTypes: Write down the exact value of sec(2π/3)
Find cosec(5π/4)
Find the exact value of cot(π/6) + sec(π/4)
State the values of x in [0, 2π] for which cot x is undefined

methods.name: Find the base ratio, then flip it
methods.summary: Find cos, sin or tan exactly with the unit circle, then take the reciprocal: sec(2π/3) = 1/(−1/2) = −2.

methods.name: Read from unit-circle coordinates
methods.summary: With P = (cos θ, sin θ), sec θ = 1/x, cosec θ = 1/y and cot θ = x/y, so signs come straight from the quadrant of P.

misconceptions: Pairing sec with sin: sec(π/3) = 1/sin(π/3) = 2/√3 instead of 2
Reading sec x as arccos x, so 'sec(1/2)' is treated as π/3
Thinking cot(π/2) is undefined because tan(π/2) is; in fact cot(π/2) = 0/1 = 0
Dropping the quadrant sign, e.g. cosec(5π/4) = √2 instead of −√2

threads.echo: sec x is 1/cos x, a reciprocal, not the inverse function arccos x: 'undoing' a number by flipping it is a different idea from undoing a process.

skills.name: Find one reciprocal ratio from another using the Pythagorean identities and the quadrant
examTypes: Given tan θ = 3/4 and π < θ < 3π/2, find sec θ
Given cot x = −2 and x is obtuse, find the exact value of cosec x
Given sec α = 3 with α acute, find tan α and sin α

methods.name: Use 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ
methods.summary: sec²θ = 1 + 9/16 = 25/16, so sec θ = ±5/4; in the third quadrant cos θ < 0, so sec θ = −5/4.

methods.name: Sketch a right triangle
methods.summary: Draw a triangle with opposite 3 and adjacent 4, find hypotenuse 5, read cos θ = 4/5, then fix the sign from the quadrant and flip.

methods.name: Point on the unit circle
methods.summary: Place a point with the given ratio in the correct quadrant on x² + y² = 1, solve for the coordinates and form the reciprocal.

misconceptions: Ignoring the quadrant: sec θ = 5/4 when θ is in the third quadrant
Using 1 + tan²θ = cosec²θ, mixing up the two identities
Writing sec²θ − 1 = −tan²θ, i.e. tan²θ = 1 − sec²θ, which gives a negative square

threads.echo: Dividing cos²θ + sin²θ = 1 by cos²θ gives 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ: the same Pythagoras fact rewritten for a different pair of ratios.

skills.name: Simplify expressions and prove identities involving sec, cosec and cot
examTypes: Show that sec x − cos x = sin x tan x
Prove that tan θ + cot θ = sec θ cosec θ
Simplify (1 − cos²x)(1 + cot²x)
Show that (1 + tan²x)/(1 + cot²x) = tan²x

methods.name: Convert to sin and cos
methods.summary: Replace every sec, cosec, cot and tan by sin and cos, combine over a common denominator and use sin²x + cos²x = 1.

methods.name: Swap with a Pythagorean identity
methods.summary: Spot 1 + tan²x or 1 + cot²x and replace it in one step by sec²x or cosec²x, then cancel.

methods.name: Work from the busier side
methods.summary: Start from the more complicated side and transform it line by line until it matches the other side.

misconceptions: Dropping the square when combining fractions: 1/cos x − cos x written as (1 − cos x)/cos x instead of (1 − cos²x)/cos x = sin²x/cos x
Cancelling across a sum, e.g. (1 + cot²x)/cot²x = 1 + 1
Treating sec²x − tan²x as 0 instead of 1

threads.echo: Each identity rewrites the same function in a new form; proving LHS = RHS is showing two forms are the same object.

skills.name: Solve equations involving reciprocal ratios, often as a quadratic in tan or cot
examTypes: Solve sec²x + tan x = 3 for 0 ≤ x ≤ π
Solve 2 cosec x = 3 + ... rearranged to a quadratic in sin x, for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π
Solve sec x = 2 for −π ≤ x ≤ π
Explain why sec x = 1/2 has no solutions

methods.name: Use an identity to get a quadratic
methods.summary: Replace sec²x by 1 + tan²x to get tan²x + tan x − 2 = 0, factorise to tan x = 1 or tan x = −2, then solve each in the interval.

methods.name: Flip to a basic ratio
methods.summary: sec x = 2 becomes cos x = 1/2; solve the basic equation and list all solutions in the interval.

methods.name: Graph both sides on the GDC
methods.summary: Plot y = sec²x + tan x and y = 3 and read every intersection in the interval, or use the graph to check the algebra.

misconceptions: Treating sec x = 2 as x = arccos 2 and concluding there are no solutions
Not noticing that |sec x| ≥ 1, so offering solutions to sec x = 1/2
Keeping only the principal value: tan x = −2 gives x = −1.11, which is outside 0 ≤ x ≤ π; the answer there is π − 1.11 ≈ 2.03

threads.echo: Each root of the quadratic in tan x is a horizontal line meeting y = tan x; counting those intersections tells you how many solutions to expect.
arctan gives one angle per value, but the equation needs every angle in the interval, so you have to add π to find the rest.

skills.name: Evaluate arcsin, arccos and arctan and their composites with principal values
examTypes: Write down arcsin(−1/2) and arccos(−1/2)
Find the exact value of sin(arccos(3/5))
Find arcsin(sin(5π/6))
Find the exact value of tan(arcsin(1/3))

methods.name: Pick the angle in the principal range
methods.summary: arcsin and arctan return an angle in [−π/2, π/2] (open for arctan), arccos in [0, π]; choose the one angle there with the right ratio.

methods.name: Draw the triangle for the inner angle
methods.summary: Let θ = arccos(3/5), so cos θ = 3/5 with θ in [0, π]; a 3-4-5 triangle gives sin θ = 4/5 (positive in that range).

methods.name: Use a Pythagorean identity
methods.summary: sin(arccos x) = √(1 − x²), taking the positive root because arccos x lies in [0, π].

misconceptions: arccos(−1/2) = −π/3, treating arccos as odd; it is π − π/3 = 2π/3
arcsin(−1/2) = 7π/6 or 11π/6, outside the range [−π/2, π/2]
arcsin(sin(5π/6)) = 5π/6, forgetting that the answer must be in the principal range (it is π/6)
Reading arcsin x as 1/sin x

threads.echo: arcsin only undoes sin after the domain is cut to [−π/2, π/2], just as √x only undoes x² on x ≥ 0.
arccos(−x) = π − arccos x is the mirror image of x on the unit circle in the y-axis, while arcsin(−x) = −arcsin x is a reflection in the x-axis.

skills.name: Sketch inverse trig graphs and state their domains and ranges, including transformed versions
examTypes: Sketch y = arctan x, showing its asymptotes
State the domain and range of f(x) = 2 arccos(x − 1)
Find the range of y = arcsin(x/2) + π/2
Explain why sin x must have its domain restricted before it has an inverse

methods.name: Reflect the restricted graph in y = x
methods.summary: Take sin x on [−π/2, π/2] (cos x on [0, π], tan x on (−π/2, π/2)) and reflect in y = x; domain and range swap.

methods.name: Transform the parent graph
methods.summary: For 2 arccos(x − 1): shift the domain [−1, 1] right by 1 to [0, 2] and stretch the range [0, π] vertically by 2 to [0, 2π].

methods.name: Plot and read off
methods.summary: Plot the function on the GDC and read the end points and asymptotes, checking against the parent ranges.

misconceptions: Drawing vertical asymptotes x = ±π/2 for arctan x instead of horizontal asymptotes y = ±π/2
Giving the range of arcsin as [0, π], copied from arccos
Stretching the domain instead of the range: saying 2 arccos(x − 1) has domain [0, 4]

threads.echo: The graph of an inverse is the reflection in y = x, so the asymptote x = π/2 of tan x becomes the asymptote y = π/2 of arctan x.
Replacing x by x − 1 moves the domain right and the factor 2 stretches the range, the same rules as for any graph.

subtopics.title: Compound angle identities
subtopics.guide: Compound angle identities for sin(A ± B), cos(A ± B) and tan(A ± B), and the double angle identity for tan. Includes deriving the double angle identities from the compound ones, with a link to De Moivre's theorem.

skills.name: Find exact values such as sin 75° or tan(π/12) by splitting into known angles
examTypes: Find the exact value of sin 75°
Show that cos(π/12) = (√6 + √2)/4
Find the exact value of tan 15° in the form a + b√3
Find the exact value of cos 105°

methods.name: Split into special angles and expand
Use a difference instead
methods.summary: Write π/12 as π/3 − π/4 (or π/4 − π/6); any split into special angles gives the same exact value.

methods.name: Work back from a double angle
methods.summary: For tan 15°, set t = tan 15° in tan 30° = 2t/(1 − t²) and take the positive root, t = 2 − √3.

misconceptions: Wrong sign in the cosine formula: cos 105° = cos 60° cos 45° + sin 60° sin 45° = (√2 + √6)/4, which is positive
Rationalising tan 15° = (√3 − 1)/(√3 + 1) wrongly to √3 − 1 instead of 2 − √3

threads.echo: sin 75° can be written through 45° + 30° or 120° − 45°; different forms of the same angle give the same exact value.

skills.name: Evaluate sin(A ± B), cos(A ± B) or tan(A ± B) from given ratios of A and B
examTypes: Given sin A = 3/5 and cos B = 5/13, both acute, find sin(A + B)
Find the exact value of cos(A + B) and hence state whether A + B is acute
Given tan A = 2 and tan B = 1/3, find tan(A − B)
Show that arctan(1/2) + arctan(1/3) = π/4

methods.name: Complete the ratios, then expand
methods.summary: Find cos A = 4/5 and sin B = 12/13 with Pythagoras, then sin(A + B) = (3/5)(5/13) + (4/5)(12/13) = 63/65.

methods.name: Two right triangles
methods.summary: Sketch a 3-4-5 and a 5-12-13 triangle, read all four ratios off them, then substitute.

methods.name: Use tan(A ± B) directly
methods.summary: When tangents are given, tan(A + B) = (tan A + tan B)/(1 − tan A tan B) avoids finding sines and cosines; (1/2 + 1/3)/(1 − 1/6) = 1.

misconceptions: Using the wrong sign in cos(A + B) and getting 56/65 instead of −16/65
Taking the negative square root for an acute angle, e.g. cos A = −4/5
tan(A + B) = tan A + tan B, which gives 5/6 instead of 1

threads.echo: Showing arctan(1/2) + arctan(1/3) = π/4 means taking tan of both sides and checking the sum lies in the principal range.

skills.name: Derive double and multiple angle identities from the compound angle formulas
examTypes: Use the formula for sin(A + B) to show that sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A
Show that tan 2θ = 2 tan θ/(1 − tan²θ)
By writing 3x = 2x + x, show that cos 3x = 4cos³x − 3cos x
Use De Moivre's theorem to confirm the formula for cos(A + B)

methods.name: Set B = A
methods.summary: Put B = A in sin(A + B), cos(A + B) and tan(A + B); then use sin²A + cos²A = 1 for the other forms of cos 2A.

methods.name: Split a multiple angle
methods.summary: cos 3x = cos(2x + x) = cos 2x cos x − sin 2x sin x; replace the double angles and sin²x = 1 − cos²x to reach 4cos³x − 3cos x.

methods.name: Multiply complex numbers
methods.summary: (cos A + i sin A)(cos B + i sin B) = cos(A + B) + i sin(A + B); comparing real and imaginary parts gives both compound formulas.

misconceptions: Writing tan 2θ = 2 tan θ/(1 + tan²θ), copying the sign from the numerator of tan(A + B)
Replacing sin²x by 1 + cos²x and getting cos 3x = −2cos³x − cos x... instead of 4cos³x − 3cos x
Assuming cos 3x = 3 cos x

threads.echo: The compound formula with B = A rewrites sin 2A in a new form; the double angle identities are special cases, not new facts.
Expanding (cos θ + i sin θ)³ with the binomial theorem and comparing real parts gives the same cos 3θ formula.

skills.name: Use the double angle identity for tan to find values and solve equations
examTypes: Given tan θ = 1/2, find tan 2θ
Use tan(π/4) = 1 to find the exact value of tan(π/8)
Solve tan 2x = 3 tan x for 0 ≤ x < π
Given tan 2α = 4/3 and α is acute, find tan α

methods.name: Form a quadratic in t = tan θ
methods.summary: For tan(π/8): 2t/(1 − t²) = 1 gives t² + 2t − 1 = 0, so t = −1 ± √2; π/8 is acute, so t = √2 − 1.

methods.name: Go through sin 2θ and cos 2θ
methods.summary: Find sin 2θ and cos 2θ from a triangle for θ and divide; slower but a good check.

misconceptions: tan 2θ = 2 tan θ, which gives 1 instead of 4/3
Keeping the negative root −1 − √2 for tan(π/8)
Dividing tan 2x = 3 tan x by tan x and losing the solution x = 0

threads.echo: The roots of t² + 2t − 1 = 0 are where y = tan(2x) meets y = 1 once x is fixed, and the graph shows which root lies in the acute range.

skills.name: Prove identities and solve equations by expanding compound angles
examTypes: Solve sin(x + π/6) = 2 cos x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π
Show that sin x + √3 cos x = 2 sin(x + π/3), and hence state its maximum value
Prove that cos(A + B) cos(A − B) = cos²A − sin²B
Show that (sin(A + B))/(cos A cos B) = tan A + tan B

methods.name: Expand and collect
methods.summary: Expand sin(x + π/6) = (√3/2) sin x + (1/2) cos x, collect to (√3/2) sin x = (3/2) cos x, so tan x = √3 and x = π/3, 4π/3.

methods.name: Read the expansion backwards
methods.summary: Spot that sin x · (1/2) + cos x · (√3/2) is sin(x + π/3), so a sum of sine and cosine collapses to one sinusoid.

methods.name: Graph both sides
methods.summary: Plot both sides on the GDC to find or check solutions, or to see that two expressions have the same graph.

misconceptions: Expanding sin(x + π/6) as sin x + 1/2
Dividing by cos x without checking cos x = 0 is not a solution
Giving only the principal solution of tan x = √3 and missing x = 4π/3

threads.echo: Once sin x + √3 cos x is written as 2 sin(x + π/3), its maximum is the amplitude 2, with no calculus needed.
sin x + √3 cos x is y = sin x translated left by π/3 and stretched vertically by 2.

subtopics.title: Relationships between trigonometric functions and the symmetry of their graphs
subtopics.guide: Relationships between the trigonometric functions shown by the symmetries of their graphs and the unit circle, such as sin(π − θ) = sin θ, cos(π − θ) = −cos θ and tan(π − θ) = −tan θ. Links to odd and even functions and to compound angles.

skills.name: Rewrite sin, cos or tan of π ± θ, π/2 ± θ or −θ in terms of θ
examTypes: Simplify cos(π − θ) + cos(π + θ)
Given sin θ = k, write sin(π + θ) and cos(π/2 − θ) in terms of k
Express tan(π − θ) in terms of tan θ
Show that sin(π/2 + θ) = cos θ

methods.name: Reflect on the unit circle
methods.summary: π − θ is the reflection of θ in the y-axis, so the y-coordinate (sin) stays and the x-coordinate (cos) changes sign.

methods.name: Expand as a compound angle
methods.summary: cos(π − θ) = cos π cos θ + sin π sin θ = −cos θ.

methods.name: Read the symmetry of the graph
methods.summary: y = sin x is symmetric about x = π/2, so sin(π − θ) = sin θ can be read straight off the graph.

misconceptions: cos(π − θ) = cos θ, copying the sine result
tan(π + θ) = −tan θ; tan has period π, so tan(π + θ) = tan θ
cos(π/2 + θ) = sin θ instead of −sin θ

threads.echo: Every related-angle identity is a reflection or rotation of the unit circle, so one quadrant of values gives all four.

skills.name: Use the odd and even properties of trig functions to simplify and classify functions
examTypes: State whether f(x) = x sin x is odd, even or neither
Simplify sin(−x) + cos(−x) + tan(−x)
Show that sec x is an even function
Use symmetry to write down the value of the integral of sin³x from −π to π

methods.name: Replace x by −x
methods.summary: Compute f(−x) using sin(−x) = −sin x and cos(−x) = cos x, then compare with f(x) and −f(x).

methods.name: Check the graph's symmetry
methods.summary: Even means mirror symmetry in the y-axis; odd means rotational symmetry of order 2 about the origin.

methods.name: Odd × odd is even
methods.summary: x and sin x are both odd, so x sin x is even; x cos x is odd × even, so it is odd.

misconceptions: Calling x sin x odd just because it contains sin x
Thinking cos x is odd because cos(π − x) = −cos x
Testing only one value, e.g. f(1) = f(−1), and concluding the function is even

threads.echo: Odd functions cancel over a symmetric interval, so the integral of sin³x from −π to π is 0 without any working.

skills.name: Use lines and centres of symmetry of trig graphs to find further solutions
examTypes: Given that sin a = 0.3 with 0 < a < π/2, find another solution of sin x = 0.3 in [0, 2π] in terms of a
State the equations of the lines of symmetry of y = cos x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π
Write down the coordinates of a centre of rotational symmetry of y = tan x
Given cos b = k, express all solutions of cos x = k in [0, 2π] in terms of b

methods.name: Mirror in a line of symmetry
methods.summary: sin x is symmetric about x = π/2, so the partner of a is π − a; cos x is symmetric about x = π, so the partner of b is 2π − b.

methods.name: Add the period
methods.summary: Add 2π for sin and cos, or π for tan, to find every further solution.

methods.name: Pairs of points on the unit circle
methods.summary: Points with equal y-coordinates are θ and π − θ; points with equal x-coordinates are θ and −θ.

misconceptions: Taking π + a as the second solution of sin x = 0.3; that gives sin x = −0.3
Placing the lines of symmetry of cos x at x = π/2 and 3π/2 (those are where it crosses the axis)
Thinking tan x has lines of symmetry

threads.echo: The second solution of a trig equation is the first one reflected in a line of symmetry of the graph.
Each solution is an intersection of y = sin x with a horizontal line, and the graph's symmetry places them in mirror pairs.

skills.name: Relate the sin, cos and tan graphs by translations and reflections
examTypes: Describe the translation that maps y = sin x onto y = cos x
Write −cos x as a sine function with a horizontal shift
Show that tan(π/2 − x) = cot x
Which of these equations has the same graph as y = sin x: y = cos(x − π/2), y = cos(x + π/2), y = −sin(−x)?

methods.name: Expand to check
methods.summary: sin(x + π/2) = sin x · 0 + cos x · 1 = cos x, so the graph of cos is the graph of sin moved left by π/2.

methods.name: Match maxima and zeros
methods.summary: sin x has its first maximum at π/2 and cos x at 0, so cos is sin translated by the vector (−π/2, 0).

methods.name: Complementary angles in a right triangle
methods.summary: In a right triangle the two acute angles are θ and π/2 − θ, so the opposite of one is the adjacent of the other: sin(π/2 − θ) = cos θ, tan(π/2 − θ) = cot θ.

misconceptions: Saying cos x is sin x translated right by π/2; sin(x − π/2) = −cos x
Treating −sin(−x) as −sin x
Thinking tan(π/2 − x) = tan x − π/2 style rewrites, i.e. distributing tan over the subtraction

threads.echo: Replacing x by x + π/2 moves the sine graph left by π/2 onto the cosine graph, the same rule as for any function.
cos x, sin(x + π/2) and −sin(x − π/2) are three forms of one graph.

subtopics.title: Vectors: concepts, components and algebra
subtopics.guide: Vectors as directed line segments, written in column form or with base vectors i, j, k. Position and displacement vectors (AB = b − a), sums, differences, scalar multiples, the zero vector, parallel vectors, magnitude, unit vectors and the distance between points, treated both algebraically and geometrically, plus proofs of geometric properties with vectors.

skills.name: Write vectors in components and find displacement vectors between points
examTypes: Write 3i − k as a column vector
Given A(1, 2, 3) and B(3, −1, 9), find the vector AB
Given OA = 2i + j and AB = i − 3j + 4k, find the coordinates of B
Find the position vector of the midpoint of AB

methods.name: End minus start
methods.summary: AB = b − a: subtract the coordinates of A from those of B component by component.

methods.name: Go via the origin
methods.summary: Travel from A back to O (−a) and then out to B (+b), so AB = −a + b.

misconceptions: AB = a − b, which reverses the direction
Writing 3i − k as (3, −1, 0), putting the k component in the j slot
Confusing the position vector of B with the displacement AB

threads.echo: AB = b − a is exactly 'how far across, how far up (and how far out)' to get from A to B.

skills.name: Add, subtract and scale vectors, and solve vector equations for unknowns
examTypes: Given a = (2, −1, 3) and b = (1, 4, 0), find 2a − 3b
Find p and q such that p(1, 2, 0) + q(0, 1, 1) = (3, 4, −2)
Draw a diagram showing a + b and a − b
Find the vector −v and explain how it relates to v on a diagram

methods.name: Work component by component
methods.summary: Scale each component, then add or subtract matching components; for unknowns, equate components to get simultaneous equations.

methods.name: Triangle and parallelogram laws
methods.summary: Place b at the tip of a to draw a + b; a − b is the diagonal from the tip of b to the tip of a.

misconceptions: Scaling only the first component: 2(2, −1, 3) = (4, −1, 3)
Drawing a − b from the tip of a to the tip of b, which is b − a
Subtracting a negative component wrongly, e.g. −1 − 12 = −11 instead of −13

threads.echo: Adding vectors is doing one move after another, the same as composing two translations of a graph.

skills.name: Find magnitudes, distances and unit vectors, and vectors of a given length
examTypes: Find |AB| for A(1, 2, 3) and B(3, −1, 9)
Find a unit vector in the direction of 2i − j + 2k
Find a vector of length 6 in the direction of (2, −1, 2)
Given |(k, 2, −2)| = 3, find the possible values of k

methods.name: Divide by the magnitude, then scale
methods.summary: Unit vector = v/|v| = (2/3, −1/3, 2/3); multiply by 6 for a vector of length 6, giving (4, −2, 4).

misconceptions: Adding components instead of squaring: |(2, −3, 6)| = 2 − 3 + 6 = 5
Squaring a negative component as negative: √(4 − 9 + 36) = √31
Missing the second root in |(k, 2, −2)| = 3: giving only k = 1, not k = ±1

threads.echo: The length of a vector is the straight-line distance of the move, the same as the 3D distance formula from SL3.1.

skills.name: Use scalar multiples to test parallel vectors and collinear points
examTypes: Find k so that (2, k, −4) is parallel to (1, 3, −2)
Show that A(1, 2, 3), B(3, 5, 4) and C(7, 11, 6) are collinear
Find the ratio AB : BC for three collinear points
Find the coordinates of D so that ABCD is a parallelogram

methods.name: Find the scalar
methods.summary: Parallel means v = kw for one k; (2, k, −4) = 2(1, 3, −2) forces k = 6.

methods.name: Parallel plus a shared point
methods.summary: If AC = 3AB, the vectors are parallel and share A, so A, B and C lie on one line.

methods.name: Equal opposite sides
methods.summary: In parallelogram ABCD, AD = BC, so d = a + c − b.

misconceptions: Concluding collinear from parallel vectors with no shared point
Using a different scalar for each component when testing for parallel
Taking ABCD in the wrong order and finding d = a + b − c, the fourth vertex of parallelogram ABDC... rather than ABCD

threads.echo: Parallel vectors are the same move scaled, just as all lines with gradient 3/4 point along (4, 3).

skills.name: Express vectors in a figure in terms of given vectors, including midpoints and ratio points
examTypes: In parallelogram OABC with OA = a and OC = c, express the vector from M, the midpoint of AB, to C in terms of a and c
P lies on AB with AP : PB = 2 : 1; find OP in terms of a and b
Express the position vector of the centroid of triangle OAB in terms of a and b

methods.name: Walk a route through known vectors
Weighted average of end points
methods.summary: A point dividing AB in m : n has position vector (na + mb)/(m + n): the nearer end gets the larger weight.

misconceptions: Swapping the weights: OP = (2/3)a + (1/3)b for AP : PB = 2 : 1
Using AP = (2/3)b instead of (2/3)(b − a)
Taking AP : PB = 2 : 1 to mean AP = 2/1 of AB

threads.echo: Any route between two points gives the same displacement, so you can always walk round the figure through vectors you know.

skills.name: Prove geometric properties using vectors
examTypes: M and N are the midpoints of OA and OB; prove that MN is parallel to AB and half its length
Prove that the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other
Prove that joining the midpoints of the sides of any quadrilateral gives a parallelogram

methods.name: Express both, then compare
methods.summary: MN = ½b − ½a = ½(b − a) = ½AB, so MN is parallel to AB and half as long.

methods.name: Two routes to one point
methods.summary: Write the intersection of the diagonals as λ along one and μ along the other, equate, and compare coefficients of independent vectors a and c to get λ = μ = ½.

misconceptions: Proving the result for one numerical example and calling it a proof
Comparing coefficients of a and b when a and b are parallel, which is not valid
Showing MN = ½AB in length only, without stating that this also proves they are parallel

threads.echo: A vector carries both length and direction, so one equation MN = ½AB proves two geometric facts at once.

subtopics.title: The scalar product and the angle between vectors
subtopics.guide: The scalar (dot) product, both in components and as v · w = |v||w| cos θ, and its algebraic properties. Using it to find the angle between vectors and to test for perpendicular vectors (v · w = 0) and parallel vectors (|v · w| = |v||w|).

skills.name: Calculate a scalar product from components or from magnitudes and the angle
examTypes: Given |a| = 4, |b| = 5 and the angle between them is 2π/3, find a · b
Find (2i − j) · (i + 3j + k)

methods.name: Use |v||w| cos θ
methods.summary: With magnitudes and the angle given, a · b = 4 × 5 × cos(2π/3) = −10.

misconceptions: Giving a vector, e.g. (3, 0, −8), instead of a number
Using sin θ instead of cos θ
Taking cos(2π/3) = 1/2 and getting +10

skills.name: Find the angle between two vectors, or an angle in a triangle given by coordinates
examTypes: Find the angle between (1, 2, 2) and (2, −1, 2)
Find angle ABC for A(1, 0, 2), B(3, 1, 0), C(2, 4, 1)
Given cos θ = −1/3, state whether the angle between the vectors is acute or obtuse

methods.name: cos θ = v · w / (|v||w|)
methods.summary: (1, 2, 2) · (2, −1, 2) = 4 and both magnitudes are 3, so cos θ = 4/9 and θ ≈ 63.6°.

methods.name: Cosine rule on the triangle
methods.summary: Find the three side lengths with the distance formula and apply the cosine rule; this gives the same angle and is a good check.

misconceptions: For angle ABC using AB and BC instead of BA and BC, which gives 180° minus the angle
Using position vectors OA and OC instead of displacement vectors from B
Forgetting to divide by both magnitudes, giving cos θ = 4

skills.name: Test for perpendicular or parallel vectors and find unknowns that make them so
examTypes: Find k so that (2, k, 3) and (1, −2, 4) are perpendicular
Show that triangle ABC has a right angle at A
Find a vector perpendicular to (3, −1, 2)
Use the scalar product to decide whether two given vectors are parallel

methods.name: Set the scalar product to zero
Compare |v · w| with |v||w|
methods.summary: For non-zero vectors, |v · w| = |v||w| exactly when cos θ = ±1, so the vectors are parallel.

methods.name: Look for a scalar multiple
methods.summary: Parallel can also be tested directly by checking whether w = kv for one k.

misconceptions: Setting the scalar product equal to 1 for perpendicular vectors
Thinking v · w = 0 means the vectors are parallel
Sign slip: 2 − 2k + 12 = 0 solved as k = −7

skills.name: Use the algebraic properties of the scalar product, including v · v = |v|², in calculations and proofs
examTypes: Given |a| = 3, |b| = 4 and a · b = 6, find |a + b|
Expand and simplify (a + b) · (a − b)
Use the scalar product to prove that the diagonals of a rhombus are perpendicular
Prove that the angle in a semicircle is a right angle

methods.name: Show the product is zero
methods.summary: For a rhombus with sides a and b, (a + b) · (b − a) = |b|² − |a|² = 0 because |a| = |b|.

methods.name: Cosine rule picture
methods.summary: |a + b|² = |a|² + |b|² + 2|a||b| cos θ is the cosine rule on the triangle formed by a, b and a + b.

misconceptions: Dropping the cross term: |a + b|² = 9 + 16, giving 5
Writing a · a = a² as a vector, or as |a| instead of |a|²

threads.echo: |a + b|² = |a|² + 2a · b + |b|² is the expansion of (x + y)² written for vectors.

subtopics.title: Vector equation of a line in two and three dimensions
subtopics.guide: The vector equation of a line r = a + λb in 2D and 3D, the meaning of the position vector a and direction vector b, and its parametric and Cartesian forms. The angle between two lines from their direction vectors, and simple kinematics with λ as time, b as velocity and |b| as speed.

skills.name: Write the vector equation of a line from two points or a point and a direction
examTypes: Find a vector equation of the line through A(1, −2, 3) and B(4, 0, 2)
Write an equation of the line through (2, 0, 5) parallel to the line r = (1, 1, 1) + λ(3, −1, 2)
Write a vector equation of the line through P perpendicular to the plane 2x − y + z = 4

methods.name: Borrow a direction
methods.summary: A parallel line reuses the other line's direction; a line perpendicular to a plane uses the plane's normal as its direction.

misconceptions: Using the position vector of B as the direction: r = a + λb instead of a + λ(b − a)
Thinking a line has only one correct equation, so rejecting r = (4, 0, 2) + μ(−3, −2, 1)
Writing r = λa + b, swapping the roles of point and direction

threads.echo: r = a + λb says: start at a, then take λ steps of the move b, the vector version of y = mx + c.

skills.name: Convert a line between vector, parametric and Cartesian forms
examTypes: Write r = (1, −2, 3) + λ(3, 2, −1) in Cartesian form
Find a point on and a direction of the line (x − 2)/3 = (1 − y)/4 = z/2
Write the line (2x − 1)/4 = y + 3 = (z − 2)/5 in vector form
Write the 2D line r = (1, 2) + λ(2, 3) in the form y = mx + c

methods.name: Make λ the subject
methods.summary: From x = 1 + 3λ, y = −2 + 2λ, z = 3 − λ, solve each for λ and set them equal: (x − 1)/3 = (y + 2)/2 = (z − 3)/(−1).

methods.name: Tidy into standard form first
methods.summary: Rewrite each fraction as (x − x₀)/l: (1 − y)/4 = (y − 1)/(−4) and (2x − 1)/4 = (x − 1/2)/2, then read the point and direction.

misconceptions: Reading (1 − y)/4 as direction component +4 instead of −4
Reading (2x − 1)/4 as point 1 and direction 4, instead of point 1/2 and direction 2
Sign of the point: reading (y + 2)/2 as y₀ = 2

threads.echo: Vector, parametric and Cartesian forms describe the same line; each makes a different feature (the point, each coordinate, or a test for membership) easiest to read.

skills.name: Test whether a point lies on a line and find points on a line with given conditions
examTypes: Determine whether (7, 2, 1) lies on r = (1, −2, 3) + λ(3, 2, −1)
The point (a, b, 0) lies on the line; find a and b
Find where the line crosses the xy-plane
Find the point on the line a distance 10 from its starting point

methods.name: Find λ from one component, check the rest
methods.summary: 1 + 3λ = 7 gives λ = 2; then −2 + 4 = 2 and 3 − 2 = 1 both match, so the point is on the line.

methods.name: Substitute into the Cartesian form
methods.summary: Check that (7 − 1)/3, (2 + 2)/2 and (1 − 3)/(−1) are all equal (they are all 2).

misconceptions: Checking only one or two components before concluding the point is on the line
Allowing a different λ for each component
Setting z = 0 by putting λ = 0

skills.name: Find the angle between two lines using their direction vectors
examTypes: Find the acute angle between the lines r = (1, 0, 2) + λ(1, 2, 2) and r = (3, 1, 0) + μ(2, −1, 2)
Show that two given lines are perpendicular
Find k if the lines with directions (1, k, 2) and (3, −1, 1) are perpendicular

methods.name: Scalar product of directions
methods.summary: cos θ = |d₁ · d₂|/(|d₁||d₂|); for (1, 2, 2) and (2, −1, 2), cos θ = 4/9 and θ ≈ 63.6°.

methods.name: Take the supplement if obtuse
methods.summary: If the formula without modulus gives an obtuse angle, the acute angle between the lines is 180° minus it.

misconceptions: Using the position vectors (1, 0, 2) and (3, 1, 0) instead of the directions
Giving the obtuse angle when the acute angle between lines is asked for
Thinking lines must intersect before an angle between them exists

skills.name: Model motion with r = a + tv: position, velocity, speed and meeting points
examTypes: A boat's position is r = (2, 1) + t(3, −4) km after t hours; find its speed
Find the time when the object is at (11, −11)
Two drones move along given lines with the same t; determine whether they collide
Find the distance between two objects after 2 hours

methods.name: Read start and velocity
methods.summary: a is the position at t = 0 and v is the velocity; speed is |v| = √(9 + 16) = 5 km/h.

methods.name: Same t for a collision
methods.summary: Set r₁(t) = r₂(t) with one shared t; if one t satisfies every component they collide, otherwise their paths may cross at different times.

methods.name: Graph the distance against time
methods.summary: Write |r₁(t) − r₂(t)| as a function of t and plot it on the GDC to read distances or the closest approach.

misconceptions: Using separate parameters t and s and concluding the objects collide because their paths cross
Taking the speed as |a| or |a + v| instead of |v|
Treating t as a distance travelled rather than a time

threads.echo: The direction vector is the velocity: how much the position changes for each unit of time, like the gradient of a displacement graph.
Each hour the boat makes the same move v, so position after t hours is the start plus t copies of v.

skills.name: Find the foot of the perpendicular from a point to a line and the shortest distance
examTypes: Find the point on the line r = (1, 0, 0) + λ(1, 1, 0) closest to P(3, 1, 2)
Hence find the shortest distance from P to the line
Find the minimum distance between two moving ships

methods.name: Make PR perpendicular to the direction
methods.summary: With R = a + λb on the line, solve PR · b = 0 for λ; here (λ − 2, λ − 1, −2) · (1, 1, 0) = 0 gives λ = 3/2 and R = (5/2, 3/2, 0).

methods.name: Minimise the squared distance
methods.summary: |PR|² is a quadratic in λ; find its minimum by completing the square or by setting its derivative to zero.

methods.name: Minimum on the GDC
methods.summary: Plot |PR| as a function of λ (or of t for moving objects) and read the minimum.

misconceptions: Setting PR · b = 0 with R = a, i.e. using the line's given point instead of the general point
Using |PA| from the given point A on the line as the shortest distance
Giving λ as the answer when the closest point's coordinates are asked for

threads.echo: The shortest distance is the minimum of a quadratic in λ, so the vertex method, calculus and the perpendicular condition all give the same point.

subtopics.title: Coincident, parallel, intersecting and skew lines
subtopics.guide: Deciding whether two lines are coincident, parallel, intersecting or skew (non-parallel and non-intersecting, possible only in 3D), and finding the point of intersection when there is one.

skills.name: Decide whether two lines are coincident, parallel, intersecting or skew
examTypes: Determine whether the lines L₁ and L₂ are parallel, intersecting or skew
Show that L₁ and L₂ are coincident
Explain why two lines in the plane cannot be skew
Order the steps of a test that classifies two lines in 3D

methods.name: Directions first, then solve
methods.summary: If the directions are multiples, test whether a point of one lies on the other (coincident) or not (parallel); if not multiples, solve for an intersection (intersecting) or show there is none (skew).

methods.name: Solve the component equations
methods.summary: Equate a₁ + λb₁ = a₂ + μb₂ in each component to get three equations in λ and μ, and read the case from how many solutions there are.

methods.name: Solve on the GDC
methods.summary: Solve two of the equations with the GDC's simultaneous equation solver, then substitute into the third.

misconceptions: Calling non-intersecting lines parallel without checking the directions (in 3D they may be skew)
Concluding coincident just because the directions are parallel
Using the same parameter λ for both lines

threads.echo: One, none or infinitely many solutions of the system is the algebra; intersecting, skew or parallel, and coincident lines is the geometry of the same fact.

skills.name: Find the point where two lines intersect
examTypes: Find the coordinates of the point of intersection of L₁ and L₂
Show that the lines intersect and find the point
Find where two lines in 2D given in vector form meet

methods.name: Solve two, check the third
methods.summary: Solve two component equations for λ and μ, check the third one is satisfied, then substitute λ into L₁ to get the point.

methods.name: Substitute parametric into Cartesian
methods.summary: Write one line in parametric form and substitute into the Cartesian equations of the other, giving equations in one parameter.

methods.name: GDC simultaneous solver
methods.summary: Enter two of the equations in the GDC solver, then verify the third by hand.

misconceptions: Not checking the third equation, so skew lines are given an 'intersection'
Substituting λ into L₂ instead of μ, which gives a point on neither line
Giving the values of λ and μ as the answer instead of the coordinates

threads.echo: The point of intersection is the solution of a system of equations, just as the intersection of two graphs solves f(x) = g(x).

skills.name: Show that two lines are skew
examTypes: Show that the lines L₁ and L₂ are skew
Explain why showing two lines do not meet is not enough to prove they are skew
Spot the error in a student's claim that two lines are skew

methods.name: Not parallel and no solution
methods.summary: Show the directions are not multiples, then solve two component equations and show the third gives a contradiction.

methods.name: Inconsistent system
methods.summary: Show the system of three equations in λ and μ has no solution, for example by elimination or the GDC, after confirming the directions are not parallel.

misconceptions: Showing only that the lines do not intersect and forgetting to show they are not parallel
Showing only that the directions are not parallel and concluding skew without checking for an intersection
Thinking skew lines can exist in 2D

skills.name: Find an unknown constant that makes two lines intersect, parallel or coincident
examTypes: Find the value of k for which L₁ and L₂ intersect
Find p and q such that the lines are coincident
For which values of a are the lines parallel?

methods.name: Solve the pair without k, then use the third
methods.summary: Find λ and μ from the two equations that do not contain k, then substitute into the third to find the k that makes it consistent.

methods.name: Force the directions to be multiples
methods.summary: For parallel lines, set one direction equal to a scalar multiple of the other and solve component by component.

misconceptions: Solving with the k equation first and getting λ in terms of k that is never pinned down
Requiring the direction vectors to be equal rather than multiples
Finding k for parallel directions and calling the lines coincident without checking a shared point

subtopics.title: The vector product
subtopics.guide: The vector (cross) product in components and as v × w = |v||w| sin θ n with n given by the right-hand rule, and its properties: anticommutative, distributive, v × v = 0, and zero for non-zero vectors exactly when they are parallel. Using |v × w| for the area of a parallelogram or triangle.

skills.name: Calculate a vector product in components
examTypes: Find (i + 2j − k) × (3i − j)
Check that a × b is perpendicular to both a and b

methods.name: 3 × 3 determinant
methods.summary: Expand the determinant with rows i j k, a, b: i(2·6 − 3·5) − j(1·6 − 3·4) + k(1·5 − 2·4) = (−3, 6, −3).

methods.name: Cyclic component pattern
methods.summary: Use (a₂b₃ − a₃b₂, a₃b₁ − a₁b₃, a₁b₂ − a₂b₁), cycling 2-3, 3-1, 1-2.

methods.name: GDC vector menu
methods.summary: Use the calculator's cross product function, then check by dotting the result with each vector.

misconceptions: Forgetting the minus on the j term: (−3, −6, −3)
Multiplying component by component: (4, 10, 18)
Giving a number instead of a vector

skills.name: Use the vector product to find a vector or unit vector perpendicular to two vectors
examTypes: Find a vector perpendicular to both (1, 2, 3) and (4, 5, 6)
Find a unit vector perpendicular to AB and AC
Use the right-hand rule to state the direction of i × j and j × i

methods.name: Cross, simplify, normalise
methods.summary: (−3, 6, −3) = −3(1, −2, 1); a unit perpendicular is (1, −2, 1)/√6 (or its negative).

methods.name: Two scalar product equations
methods.summary: Let n = (x, y, z) with n · a = 0 and n · b = 0, choose one component and solve for the others.

methods.name: Right-hand rule
methods.summary: Point the fingers along v, curl towards w; the thumb gives the direction of v × w, so i × j = k and j × i = −k.

misconceptions: Dividing by the magnitude of one of the original vectors instead of the cross product's magnitude
Thinking there is only one perpendicular unit vector, forgetting its negative
Thinking i × j = −k

skills.name: Find areas of parallelograms and triangles with |v × w|
examTypes: Find the area of the triangle with vertices A(1, 0, 2), B(2, 2, 5), C(5, 5, 8)
Find the area of the parallelogram with sides a and b
Given the area of triangle ABC, find the unknown coordinate k

methods.name: Half the cross product
methods.summary: AB = (1, 2, 3), AC = (4, 5, 6); AB × AC = (−3, 6, −3) with magnitude √54 = 3√6, so the triangle's area is 3√6/2.

methods.name: ½ab sin C
methods.summary: Find |AB|, |AC| and angle A with the scalar product, then use ½|AB||AC| sin A; longer but the same result.

misconceptions: Forgetting the ½ for a triangle: 3√6 instead of 3√6/2
Using position vectors a × b instead of AB × AC
Taking AB × BC × CA style triple products, or using sides that do not share a vertex

threads.echo: The magnitude of v × w measures the area swept out by v and w, linking the vector product to area just as ½ab sin C did.

skills.name: Use the properties of the vector product and |v × w| = |v||w| sin θ
examTypes: Simplify (a + b) × (a − b) in terms of a × b
Given |a| = 2, |b| = 5 and a · b = 6, find |a × b|
Explain why a × b = 0 for non-zero vectors means they are parallel
True or false: a × b = b × a

methods.name: Expand and use b × a = −a × b
methods.summary: (a + b) × (a − b) = a × a − a × b + b × a − b × b = −2(a × b), since a × a = b × b = 0.

methods.name: Find sin θ from cos θ
|a × b|² + (a · b)² = |a|²|b|²
methods.summary: This follows from sin²θ + cos²θ = 1: |a × b|² = 100 − 36 = 64, so |a × b| = 8.

misconceptions: (a + b) × (a − b) = a × a − b × b = 0, treating it like a difference of squares
Taking a × a = |a|² instead of 0
Using cos θ in place of sin θ, which gives |a × b| = 6

threads.echo: |a × b| and a · b are the sin and cos parts of the same angle, so knowing one fixes the other, as sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 promises.

subtopics.title: Vector and Cartesian equations of a plane
subtopics.guide: Equations of a plane in vector form r = a + λb + μc (b, c non-parallel vectors in the plane), scalar product form r · n = a · n with normal n, and Cartesian form ax + by + cz = d.

skills.name: Write a plane in the form r = a + λb + μc from points or lines
examTypes: Write a vector equation of the plane through A(1, 0, 0), B(0, 2, 0) and C(0, 0, 3)
Find a vector equation of the plane containing the line L and the point P
Find a vector equation of the plane containing two intersecting lines

methods.name: Reuse a line's direction
methods.summary: For a plane containing line L and point P, use a point on L, L's direction and the vector from that point to P.

misconceptions: Using position vectors b and c as directions instead of b − a and c − a
Choosing two parallel direction vectors, which only describe a line
Using the same parameter for both directions: r = a + λ(b + c)

threads.echo: Every point of the plane is reached from a by some number of steps along b and some along c: two independent moves.

skills.name: Find the Cartesian equation of a plane from a normal and a point, or from three points
examTypes: Find the Cartesian equation of the plane through A(1, 0, 0), B(0, 2, 0), C(0, 0, 3)
Find the equation of the plane through (3, 0, 1) with normal (1, −2, 2)
Write the plane in the form r · n = d

methods.name: Cross two directions for the normal
Substitute the points
methods.summary: Put each point into ax + by + cz = d to get equations, fix one coefficient and solve; here it gives x + y/2 + z/3 = 1.

misconceptions: Using d = |n| or d = 0 instead of d = n · a
Sign slip in the cross product, giving a vector that is not perpendicular to both directions
Taking the position vector of a point as the normal

threads.echo: 6x + 3y + 2z = 6 and x/1 + y/2 + z/3 = 1 are the same plane; the second form shows the intercepts directly.

skills.name: Convert a plane between vector, scalar product and Cartesian forms
examTypes: Convert r = (1, 2, 0) + λ(1, 0, 1) + μ(0, 1, −1) to Cartesian form
Write a normal vector to the plane 2x − y + 3z = 7
Write the plane x + y + z = 3 in parametric form
Match each plane equation to its normal vector

methods.name: Cross the directions
methods.summary: From vector form, n = b × c and d = a · n give the Cartesian equation.

methods.name: Eliminate λ and μ
methods.summary: Write x, y, z in terms of λ and μ and eliminate both to get one linear equation.

misconceptions: Reading the normal from ax + by + cz = d as (a, b, d)
Thinking the normal is one of the direction vectors in the vector form
Including d as a fourth component or thinking a plane has a unique vector form

threads.echo: The vector form is best for generating points, the Cartesian form for testing them; both describe the same plane.

skills.name: Use normals to test points and build planes parallel or perpendicular to given objects
examTypes: Determine whether (2, −1, 4) lies on the plane 3x + y − z = 1
Find the plane through (1, 1, 1) parallel to 2x − y + 3z = 5
Find the plane through P perpendicular to the line r = a + λ(1, −2, 2)
Find k if the point (k, 2, 1) lies on the plane

methods.name: Keep the normal, change d
methods.summary: A parallel plane has the same normal: 2x − y + 3z = d, and the point (1, 1, 1) gives d = 4.

methods.name: Line direction as normal
methods.summary: A plane perpendicular to a line has the line's direction as its normal.

methods.name: Substitute the point
methods.summary: Put the coordinates into the left side and compare with d.

misconceptions: Keeping d = 5 for the parallel plane, which gives the same plane
Using the line direction as a vector in the plane instead of as its normal
Thinking planes with normals (2, −1, 3) and (4, −2, 6) are not parallel

subtopics.title: Intersections and angles between lines and planes
subtopics.guide: Intersections of a line with a plane, of two planes and of three planes, found by solving equations and interpreted geometrically (a point, a line, a plane, or no intersection), linking to systems of linear equations. The angle between a line and a plane and between two planes.

skills.name: Find where a line meets a plane, or show it is parallel to or lies in the plane
examTypes: Find the point where r = (1, 2, 0) + λ(2, −1, 1) meets x + y + z = 7
Show that the line is parallel to the plane and does not meet it
Show that the line lies in the plane

methods.name: Substitute the parametric form
methods.summary: (1 + 2λ) + (2 − λ) + λ = 7 gives λ = 2, so the point is (5, 0, 2).

methods.name: Test d · n first
methods.summary: If d · n ≠ 0 there is one intersection point; if d · n = 0 the line is parallel, and it lies in the plane exactly when one of its points does.

misconceptions: Giving λ = 2 as the answer instead of the point (5, 0, 2)
Reading 0 = 4 after substitution as λ = 0
Reading 0 = 0 as 'no intersection' instead of 'the line lies in the plane'

threads.echo: One solution, no solution or infinitely many for λ is the algebra of a line that crosses, misses or lies in the plane.

skills.name: Find the line of intersection of two planes
examTypes: Find a vector equation of the line of intersection of x + y + z = 6 and x − y + 2z = 5
Show that two given planes are parallel and do not meet
Find the direction of the line where two planes meet

methods.name: Cross the normals, then find a point
methods.summary: Direction n₁ × n₂ = (3, −1, −2); setting z = 0 gives x + y = 6 and x − y = 5, so the point (11/2, 1/2, 0) is on the line.

methods.name: Let one variable be λ
methods.summary: Set z = λ, solve the two equations for x and y in terms of λ, and read off the line.

methods.name: Row-reduce on the GDC
methods.summary: Row-reduce the 2 × 4 augmented matrix and read x and y in terms of the free variable.

misconceptions: Using n₁ + n₂ or one of the normals as the line's direction
Setting z = 0 when the line has z constant, so no point with z = 0 exists
Thinking two non-parallel planes can fail to meet

threads.echo: Two equations in three unknowns leave one free parameter, and geometrically that free parameter traces the line where the planes cross.

skills.name: Find and interpret the intersection of three planes, including the cases with no unique point
examTypes: Find the point of intersection of three given planes
Find the value of k for which the three planes do not meet at a single point
For that value of k, show that the planes meet in a line and find its equation
Describe the geometric arrangement when the system has no solution

methods.name: Elimination
methods.summary: Eliminate variables (or row-reduce by hand) to triangular form; a row 0 = 0 means a line (sheaf) and a row 0 = c ≠ 0 means no common point.

methods.name: GDC solver or RREF
methods.summary: Enter the augmented matrix and read a unique solution, a parameter, or an inconsistency.

methods.name: Look at the normals
methods.summary: Parallel normals mean parallel planes; if no two are parallel and there is no single point, the planes form a sheaf (common line) or a triangular prism.

misconceptions: Assuming 'no unique solution' means 'no solution', missing the sheaf case
Thinking that when there is no common point, two of the planes must be parallel (the triangular prism has no parallel planes)
Dividing by an expression in k such as k − 2 without treating k = 2 separately

threads.echo: The number of solutions of a 3 × 3 system (one, infinitely many, none) is read geometrically as a point, a line or plane, or a prism or parallel planes.

skills.name: Find the angle between a line and a plane
examTypes: Find the acute angle between the line r = (1, 0, 2) + λ(2, 1, −2) and the plane x + 2y + 2z = 5
Find the angle between the line AB and the plane
Explain why the scalar product of direction and normal gives 90° minus the required angle

methods.name: Use sin with the normal
methods.summary: sin θ = |d · n|/(|d||n|), because the angle between the line and the normal is 90° − θ.

methods.name: Find the angle to the normal, then subtract
methods.summary: Find φ between d and n with the cosine formula, then the angle with the plane is 90° − φ.

misconceptions: Giving the angle between the line and the normal instead of the plane
Using a direction vector lying in the plane in place of the normal
Leaving an obtuse answer without taking the acute angle

skills.name: Find the angle between two planes
examTypes: Find the acute angle between the planes 2x − y + z = 3 and x + y + 2z = 1
Show that two given planes are perpendicular
Find k if the planes x + ky + z = 2 and 2x − y + 3z = 0 are perpendicular

methods.name: Angle between the normals
methods.summary: cos θ = |n₁ · n₂|/(|n₁||n₂|); for (2, −1, 1) and (1, 1, 2), n₁ · n₂ = 3 and |n₁| = |n₂| = √6, so cos θ = 1/2 and θ = 60°.

methods.name: Edge-on view
methods.summary: Looking along the line of intersection, the two planes appear as lines and their normals turn through the same angle as the planes.

misconceptions: Using sin instead of cos, as for a line and a plane
Taking the angle between the constants or the position vectors of points on the planes
Giving 120° when the acute angle is asked for

skills.name: Find the foot of the perpendicular from a point to a plane, the distance and the reflected point
examTypes: Find the point on the plane x + y + z = 7 closest to P(1, 2, 0)
Hence find the shortest distance from P to the plane
Find the reflection of P in the plane

methods.name: Normal line through the point
methods.summary: Write r = p + λn, find where it meets the plane (the foot F), then the distance is |PF| and the image is P′ = 2F − P.

methods.name: Distance by projection
methods.summary: The distance from P to n · r = d is |n · p − d|/|n|, the length of the component of a vector from the plane to P along the unit normal.

misconceptions: Using a line through P that is not along the normal
Giving the foot F as the reflection instead of 2F − P
Forgetting to divide by |n|, which gives |n · p − d| as the distance

threads.echo: The plane is a mirror: the foot of the perpendicular is the midpoint of P and its image.
The shortest distance is along the normal, the 3D version of the perpendicular being the shortest route to a line.

subtopics.title: Bayes' theorem
subtopics.guide: Using Bayes' theorem to reverse a conditional probability, with at most three events in the partition, for example in medical testing where a test result is used to update the chance of having a disease. Builds on conditional probability and independence from SL.

skills.name: Reverse a conditional probability with Bayes' theorem for two events
examTypes: Given P(A), P(B | A) and P(B | A′), find P(A | B)
Given that it rained, find the probability that the forecast predicted rain
A student was late; find the probability they came by bus

methods.name: Tree diagram: wanted branch over all B branches
methods.summary: Multiply along each branch ending in B, then divide the A-and-B branch by the sum of all B branches.

methods.name: Imagine 100 or 1000 cases
methods.summary: Turn the probabilities into counts in a two-way table and read the fraction of B cases that are also A.

misconceptions: Gives P(B | A) = 0.8 as the answer for P(A | B)
Gives the joint probability P(A ∩ B) = 0.24 without dividing by P(B)
Divides by P(B | A) + P(B | A′) = 1.2 instead of P(B) = 0.52

skills.name: Apply Bayes' theorem with a partition of three events
examTypes: Three machines make 50%, 30% and 20% of the items with defect rates 2%, 3% and 5%; given an item is defective, find the probability it came from the third machine
Find the probability that a randomly chosen item is defective
Given that a customer bought a ticket, find the probability they came from each of three regions

methods.name: Three-branch tree
methods.summary: Draw three first-stage branches, multiply along each defective path and take the required path's share of the total.

methods.name: Count out of 1000 items
methods.summary: 1000 items give 10, 9 and 10 defectives from the three machines, so 10 of the 29 defectives come from the third.

misconceptions: Ignores the production shares and gives 0.05/(0.02 + 0.03 + 0.05) = 0.5
Gives P(D | C) = 0.05 instead of P(C | D)
Forgets one branch in the total, e.g. divides by 0.019

skills.name: Interpret a diagnostic test with Bayes' theorem
examTypes: A disease affects 1% of people; a test detects it 95% of the time and gives a false positive 10% of the time. Find the probability that a person who tests positive has the disease
Explain why most positive results are false positives for a rare disease
Find the probability that a person who tests negative does not have the disease

methods.name: Natural frequencies
methods.summary: In 10 000 people, 100 have the disease and 95 test positive; 9900 do not and 990 test positive; so 95 of 1085 positives are true.

methods.name: Tree diagram
methods.summary: Branch first on disease status, then on test result, and compare the true-positive path with all positive paths.

misconceptions: Gives the sensitivity 0.95 as P(disease | positive)
Gives 0.90 or 0.10 by using the specificity or false-positive rate directly
Gives the joint probability 0.0095 without dividing by P(positive)

skills.name: Find an unknown prior or conditional probability from a Bayes result
examTypes: P(A | B) = 0.6, P(B | A) = 0.9 and P(B | A′) = 0.2; find P(A)
Find the false-positive rate that would make P(disease | positive) at least 0.5
Show that P(A | B) = P(A) when A and B are independent

methods.name: Write Bayes with the unknown and solve
GDC equation solver
methods.summary: Enter the Bayes expression with the unknown and solve numerically, or graph it against the target value.

methods.name: Table of counts with an unknown
methods.summary: Fill a two-way table with 100p and 100(1 − p) cases, express the required fraction and solve.

misconceptions: Writes P(B | A′) as 1 − P(B | A), using 0.1 instead of 0.2
Uses p instead of 1 − p for P(A′) in the denominator
Sets P(A ∩ B) equal to 0.6 instead of P(A | B)

subtopics.title: Discrete and continuous random variables: pdfs, mean, variance, median and mode
subtopics.guide: Variance of discrete random variables, and continuous random variables defined by probability density functions (including piecewise ones) that integrate to 1. Covers the mode and median of a continuous variable, E(X), E(X²), Var(X) = E(X²) − [E(X)]² and standard deviation for both types, fair games, and the effect of the linear transformation aX + b.

skills.name: Find the variance and standard deviation of a discrete random variable
examTypes: Find Var(X) for the probability distribution in the table
Find E(X²) and hence the standard deviation of X
Given E(X) = 2 and Var(X) = 1.5, find the unknown values in the table

methods.name: Var(X) = Σ(x − μ)²P(X = x)
methods.summary: Subtract the mean from each value, square, weight by its probability and add.

methods.name: GDC 1-Var Stats with probabilities as frequencies
methods.summary: Put values in one list and probabilities in another; σx is the standard deviation, so square it for the variance.

misconceptions: Computes E(X²) as [E(X)]², so the variance comes out as 0
Calculates Σx²P(X = x) − E(X) = 1.7 − 1.1 = 0.6 instead of 0.49
Gives the variance 0.49 when the standard deviation 0.7 was asked for
Squares the probabilities instead of the values when finding E(X²)

threads.echo: For a distribution symmetric about its mean, the mean comes free from the symmetry, leaving only the spread to calculate.

skills.name: Find an unknown constant so that a function is a valid pdf
examTypes: f(x) = kx(4 − x) for 0 ≤ x ≤ 4 and 0 otherwise; find k
Find k for the piecewise pdf f(x) = kx for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2, k(4 − x) for 2 < x ≤ 4
Explain why f(x) = x − 1 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2 cannot be a pdf

methods.name: Set the total integral equal to 1
Use the area of a shape
methods.summary: The piecewise pdf is a triangle with base 4 and height 2k, so its area 4k = 1 and k = 1/4.

methods.name: GDC numerical integral
methods.summary: Integrate the function without k on the GDC and take k as the reciprocal of the result.

misconceptions: Sets the maximum value of f equal to 1 instead of the total area
Integrates only the first piece of a piecewise pdf, giving k = 1/2 instead of 1/4
Uses only the area condition for f(x) = k(x − 1) on [0, 3] and gives k = 2/3, missing that f is then negative for x < 1, so no valid k exists

threads.echo: Total probability 1 is a total area under a curve, the continuous version of adding the probabilities in a table.

skills.name: Find probabilities from a probability density function
examTypes: Find P(1 < X < 3) for a piecewise pdf
Find P(X < 1 | X < 2)

methods.name: Integrate the pdf between the limits
GDC definite integral
methods.summary: Use the numerical integration tool on Paper 2, splitting at the joins of a piecewise pdf.

methods.name: Use symmetry of the pdf
methods.summary: If the pdf is symmetric about x = 2, then P(X < 2) = 1/2 and P(X < 1) = P(X > 3).

misconceptions: Gives f(1) = 9/32 as P(X = 1) or as P(X < 1)
Thinks P(X ≤ 1) and P(X < 1) differ for a continuous variable
For P(X < 1 | X < 2) gives P(X < 1) = 5/32 instead of (5/32)/(1/2) = 5/16

threads.echo: A probability for a continuous variable is an area under the pdf, built by adding up thin strips f(x)dx.
A pdf symmetric about x = c splits its area equally, so P(X < c) = 1/2 without integrating.

skills.name: Find E(X), Var(X) and the standard deviation of a continuous random variable
examTypes: Find E(X) for the pdf f(x) = (3/32)x(4 − x), 0 ≤ x ≤ 4
Find E(X²) and hence Var(X)
Find the standard deviation of X for a piecewise pdf

methods.name: E(X) = ∫x f(x) dx, E(X²) = ∫x² f(x) dx
Mean from symmetry
methods.summary: If the pdf is symmetric about x = c, E(X) = c without integrating.

methods.name: GDC integrals
methods.summary: Evaluate ∫x f(x) dx and ∫x² f(x) dx numerically, splitting a piecewise pdf at its joins.

misconceptions: Computes E(X) as ∫f(x) dx, which always gives 1
Uses Var(X) = E(X²) − E(X) and gets 24/5 − 2 = 14/5
Integrates x f(x) over only one piece of a piecewise pdf

threads.echo: E(X) = ∫x f(x) dx is the continuous version of Σx P(X = x): weighted values added up as an integral.
A pdf symmetric about x = c has mean c, just as a symmetric probability table does.

skills.name: Find the median and mode of a continuous random variable
examTypes: Find the median of X where f(x) = x/2 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2
Find the mode of X for the given pdf
Find the median of a piecewise pdf, stating which piece it lies in

methods.name: Solve ∫ up to m of f(x) dx = 1/2
methods.summary: For f(x) = x/2 on [0, 2]: m²/4 = 1/2, so m = √2 (rejecting −√2, which is outside the domain).

methods.name: Check the first piece's area first
methods.summary: For a piecewise pdf, find the area of the first piece: if it is more than 1/2 the median lies in it, otherwise in a later piece.

methods.name: Mode where f is greatest
methods.summary: Solve f′(x) = 0 and compare with the end points and joins; for f(x) = x/2 on [0, 2] the maximum is at the end point, so the mode is 2.

methods.name: GDC solver and maximum
methods.summary: Solve the integral equation numerically and use the graph maximum tool for the mode.

misconceptions: Gives the median as the midpoint of the interval, 1, instead of √2
Looks only for f′(x) = 0 and says there is no mode when the maximum is at an end point
Solves for the median in the wrong piece of a piecewise pdf and gets a value outside that piece
Confuses the median with the mean and integrates x f(x) instead

threads.echo: The mode is the highest point of the pdf, found by f′(x) = 0 or at an end point, the same check as any maximum problem.
The median is where the accumulated area reaches exactly half.

skills.name: Use E(aX + b) and Var(aX + b), including in fair games
examTypes: Given E(X) = 4 and Var(X) = 2, find E(3X − 5) and Var(3X − 5)
Prizes are paid as £(5X − 2); find the expected gain and decide whether the game is fair
Temperatures in °C have mean 20 and standard deviation 3; find the mean and standard deviation in °F

methods.name: E(aX + b) = aE(X) + b, Var(aX + b) = a²Var(X)
methods.summary: E(3X − 5) = 3(4) − 5 = 7 and Var(3X − 5) = 9(2) = 18, so the standard deviation is 3√2.

methods.name: Shift and stretch the distribution
methods.summary: Adding b moves every value and the mean by b but leaves the spread; multiplying by a scales every distance from the mean by |a|.

methods.name: Build the new distribution directly
methods.summary: For a discrete X, transform every value in the table and recompute E and Var to check the formulas.

methods.name: Fair means expected gain zero
methods.summary: Write the gain as a linear function of X and set E(gain) = 0 to find a fair stake or prize.

misconceptions: Gives Var(3X − 5) = 3 × 2 − 5 = 1 by applying the mean rule to the variance
Gives Var(3X − 5) = 9 × 2 − 5 = 13, subtracting b from the variance
Gives Var(−2X) = −8 instead of 8, or the standard deviation of −2X as negative
Calls a game fair when the expected payout is zero, ignoring the stake

threads.echo: aX + b moves the mean by the same rule as a graph translation and stretch, and the variance ignores the shift, just as standardising does.

subtopics.title: Continuity, differentiability, limits and differentiation from first principles
subtopics.guide: An informal sense of continuity and differentiability at a point (never tested formally), limits as convergence or divergence, and the derivative defined from first principles as the limit of (f(x + h) − f(x))/h, used for polynomials only. Higher derivatives with the notations dⁿy/dxⁿ and f⁽ⁿ⁾(x), including nth-derivative patterns proved by induction.

skills.name: Decide informally whether a function is continuous or differentiable at a point
examTypes: From the graph, state whether f is continuous at x = 2
Explain why y = |x − 1| is not differentiable at x = 1
Which of these graphs shows a function that is continuous but not differentiable at the origin?

methods.name: Look for breaks and corners
methods.summary: Continuous means the graph can be drawn through the point without lifting the pen; differentiable also needs a single smooth tangent there, so no corner, cusp or vertical tangent.

methods.name: Compare left and right gradients
methods.summary: Work out the gradient just to the left and just to the right of the point; if they differ (as with |x|, −1 and +1), the function is not differentiable there.

misconceptions: Believing continuous implies differentiable, so |x| has derivative 0 at x = 0
Calling (x² − 1)/(x − 1) continuous at x = 1 because its limit there is 2, although f(1) is undefined
Treating a vertical tangent, such as y = x^(1/3) at the origin, as a point where the derivative exists

threads.echo: A derivative is a single 'how fast' at a point; at a corner the rate from the left and the rate from the right disagree, so there is no one answer.

skills.name: Evaluate limits and decide convergence or divergence
examTypes: Find the limit of (x² − 9)/(x − 3) as x → 3
Determine whether the sequence uₙ = (2n + 1)/(n + 4) converges, and state its limit
Explain why the limit of 1.2ⁿ as n → ∞ does not exist

methods.name: Simplify, then substitute
methods.summary: Factorise and cancel the common factor that makes 0/0, e.g. (x² − 9)/(x − 3) = x + 3, then substitute to get 6.

methods.name: Divide by the highest power
methods.summary: For n → ∞, divide top and bottom by the highest power of n: (2 + 1/n)/(1 + 4/n) → 2.

methods.name: Table of values
methods.summary: Tabulate values ever closer to the point (or ever larger n) on the GDC and watch where they settle; good for checking, not a proof.

methods.name: Use |r| < 1 for powers
methods.summary: rⁿ → 0 when |r| < 1 and diverges when |r| > 1, the same condition as for a geometric series to have a sum to infinity.

misconceptions: Stopping at 0/0 and saying the limit is 0 or does not exist, instead of 6 for (x² − 9)/(x − 3) at x = 3
Taking the ratio of constant terms for n → ∞: (2n + 1)/(n + 4) → 1/4 instead of 2
Thinking every sequence whose terms keep changing must diverge, so (−0.5)ⁿ is said to diverge

threads.echo: Repeated multiplication by r shrinks to 0 exactly when |r| < 1, the same test that decides whether a geometric series converges.

skills.name: Differentiate a polynomial from first principles
examTypes: Use the definition of the derivative to find f′(x) for f(x) = 3x² − 5x
Show from first principles that the derivative of x³ is 3x²
Find the gradient of y = x² + 4 at x = 1 from first principles

methods.name: Expand, cancel h, take the limit
methods.summary: Write f(x + h), expand, subtract f(x) so every remaining term has a factor h, divide by h, then let h → 0.

methods.name: Chord gradients shrinking to a point
methods.summary: Compute gradients of chords from x to x + h for h = 0.1, 0.01, 0.001 and see them approach f′(x); this supports the answer but does not replace the algebra.

methods.name: Check with the power rule
methods.summary: Differentiate normally to know the target answer, then make sure the first-principles working reaches it.

misconceptions: Expanding (x + h)³ as x³ + h³, which gives a derivative of 0 for x³
Replacing x by x + h in only some terms: f(x + h) = 3(x + h)² − 5x gives f′(x) = 6x instead of 6x − 5
Substituting h = 0 before cancelling, which leaves the meaningless 0/0

threads.echo: First principles turns the gradient of a chord, rise over run, into the gradient of the tangent by letting the run h shrink to 0.

skills.name: Find higher derivatives and spot the pattern for f⁽ⁿ⁾(x)
examTypes: Find d³y/dx³ for y = x⁴ − 2x² + 7
Given f(x) = e^(3x), write down an expression for f⁽ⁿ⁾(x)
Find f⁽¹⁰⁾(x) for f(x) = sin x

methods.name: Differentiate repeatedly
methods.summary: Differentiate the previous result each time and keep the coefficients unsimplified so the pattern stays visible.

methods.name: Use a repeating cycle
methods.summary: Derivatives of sin x repeat every four steps (cos, −sin, −cos, sin), so f⁽ⁿ⁾ depends only on n mod 4: f⁽¹⁰⁾ = f⁽²⁾ = −sin x.

methods.name: Track the factor each step
methods.summary: Each derivative of e^(kx) multiplies by k, so f⁽ⁿ⁾(x) = kⁿe^(kx).

misconceptions: Reading f⁽ⁿ⁾(x) as the power [f(x)]ⁿ
Writing the nth derivative of e^(3x) as 3n·e^(3x) instead of 3ⁿe^(3x)
Treating d²y/dx² as (dy/dx)²

threads.echo: Each derivative of e^(kx) multiplies by k again, so the nth derivative carries kⁿ: repeated differentiation is repeated multiplication.

skills.name: Prove a formula for the nth derivative by induction
examTypes: Prove by induction that dⁿ/dxⁿ (x eˣ) = (x + n)eˣ for all n ∈ ℤ⁺
Conjecture a formula for f⁽ⁿ⁾(x) when f(x) = 1/x and prove it by induction
Find the first three derivatives of x e^(2x), then prove the general result

methods.name: Differentiate the assumed case
methods.summary: Check n = 1, assume the result for n = k, differentiate that expression once to reach the n = k + 1 form, then write the concluding statement.

methods.name: Conjecture from the first few cases
methods.summary: Work out f′, f″ and f‴, keep factorials and signs unsimplified (e.g. (−1)ⁿn!/xⁿ⁺¹ for 1/x), and read off the general form before proving it.

misconceptions: Checking n = 1, 2, 3 and calling that a proof
Starting from the n = k + 1 statement and working backwards as if it were already known
Losing the alternating sign: claiming the nth derivative of 1/x is n!/xⁿ⁺¹

threads.echo: Each step of the induction is one more 'rate of change of the rate of change': the k + 1 case is the derivative of the k case.

subtopics.title: Limits by l'Hôpital's rule or Maclaurin series
subtopics.guide: Limits of quotients f(x)/g(x) as x → a or x → ∞ that give the indeterminate forms 0/0 or ∞/∞, found with l'Hôpital's rule (applied more than once if needed) or by Maclaurin series. Includes the standard result sin θ/θ → 1 as θ → 0 and links to horizontal asymptotes.

skills.name: Recognise an indeterminate form and whether l'Hôpital's rule applies
examTypes: Show that the limit of (eˣ − 1)/x as x → 0 is of indeterminate form
Which of these limits can be found by direct substitution, and which need l'Hôpital's rule?
Explain why l'Hôpital's rule cannot be used for the limit of (x + 1)/(x + 2) as x → 0

methods.name: Substitute first
methods.summary: Put x = a into the numerator and denominator separately; only 0/0 or ∞/∞ means more work is needed, otherwise the value (or divergence) is the answer.

methods.name: Compare growth as x → ∞
methods.summary: For x → ∞, decide whether each part tends to infinity; exponentials beat powers and powers beat logarithms, which predicts the answer.

misconceptions: Applying l'Hôpital to (x + 1)/(x + 2) at x = 0 to get 1 instead of 1/2
Treating 5/0 as an indeterminate form instead of a divergent limit
Thinking 0/0 means the limit is 0

threads.echo: Substituting tells you the form; graphing the quotient near x = a tells you where it is heading, and the two should agree once the limit is found.

skills.name: Find a 0/0 limit with l'Hôpital's rule
examTypes: Use l'Hôpital's rule to find the limit of sin 4x / x as x → 0
Find the limit of ln x / (x − 1) as x → 1
Find the limit of (2ˣ − 1)/x as x → 0

methods.name: Differentiate top and bottom separately
methods.summary: Replace f(x)/g(x) by f′(x)/g′(x) and substitute again: sin 4x / x becomes 4 cos 4x / 1 → 4.

methods.name: Leading terms of the series
methods.summary: Replace each function by its first non-zero Maclaurin terms: sin 4x ≈ 4x, so sin 4x / x → 4.

methods.name: Rescale to sin θ/θ
methods.summary: Write sin 4x / x = 4 × sin 4x / (4x) and use sin θ/θ → 1.

methods.name: Table near the point
methods.summary: Tabulate the quotient for x = ±0.01, ±0.001 to confirm the value.

misconceptions: Using the quotient rule on f/g instead of differentiating f and g separately
Giving sin 4x / x → 1, ignoring the 4
Forgetting ln 2 when differentiating 2ˣ, so (2ˣ − 1)/x → 1 instead of ln 2

threads.echo: Near x = a both top and bottom behave like their tangent lines, so the limit is the ratio of their rates of change, f′(a)/g′(a).

skills.name: Find limits as x → ∞ of ∞/∞ form
examTypes: Find the limit of x² / eˣ as x → ∞
Find the limit of ln x / √x as x → ∞
Hence write down the equation of the horizontal asymptote of y = (3x² + 1)/(x² − 4)

methods.name: l'Hôpital's rule
methods.summary: Differentiate top and bottom until the form is no longer ∞/∞: x²/eˣ → 2x/eˣ → 2/eˣ → 0.

methods.name: Divide by the highest power
methods.summary: For rational functions, divide every term by the highest power of x: (3 + 1/x²)/(1 − 4/x²) → 3.

methods.name: Graph and zoom out
methods.summary: Graph the function over a large window and read the level it settles to, as a check.

misconceptions: Writing ∞/∞ = 1, so the limit of x²/eˣ is claimed to be 1
Thinking a power always beats an exponential and giving ∞ for x²/eˣ
Stopping after one application when the result 2x/eˣ is still ∞/∞

threads.echo: Repeated multiplication eventually beats any power of x, which is why xⁿ/eˣ → 0 however large n is.

skills.name: Apply l'Hôpital's rule repeatedly
examTypes: Find the limit of (1 − cos x)/x² as x → 0
Find the limit of (x − sin x)/x³ as x → 0
Find the limit of (eˣ − 1 − x)/x² as x → 0

methods.name: Repeat until substitution works
methods.summary: Check the form after each application and stop as soon as it is determinate: (x − sin x)/x³ → (1 − cos x)/3x² → sin x/6x → cos x/6 → 1/6.

methods.name: Expand with Maclaurin series
methods.summary: x − sin x = x³/6 − x⁵/120 + …, so dividing by x³ gives 1/6 − x²/120 + … → 1/6.

methods.name: Finish with a known limit
methods.summary: After one or two applications, recognise a standard limit such as sin x/x → 1 and use it instead of differentiating again.

misconceptions: Stopping at sin x/(6x), writing 0/0 = 0 instead of 1/6
Applying the rule again to a determinate form, e.g. differentiating cos x/6 to get −sin x/0
Sign slip in the second derivative: (1 − cos x)/x² → −1/2 instead of 1/2

threads.echo: l'Hôpital and the Maclaurin expansion rewrite the same quotient in different forms; both must give 1/6, so one checks the other.

skills.name: Use Maclaurin series to evaluate a limit
examTypes: Use the Maclaurin series for e^(x²) to find the limit of (e^(x²) − 1)/x² as x → 0
By expanding ln(1 + x), find the limit of (ln(1 + x) − x)/x² as x → 0
Use series to find the limit of (sin x − x cos x)/x³ as x → 0

methods.name: Expand, cancel, let x → 0
methods.summary: Expand to enough terms that the lowest power survives, divide by the denominator, then let x → 0: (ln(1 + x) − x)/x² = −1/2 + x/3 − … → −1/2.

methods.name: l'Hôpital as a check
methods.summary: Differentiate top and bottom (as often as needed) and confirm the same value.

misconceptions: Truncating too early: using sin x ≈ x and cos x ≈ 1 makes sin x − x cos x ≈ 0 and gives 0 instead of 1/3
Expanding ln(1 + x) only as far as x, so the numerator is 0 and the limit is given as 0 instead of −1/2
Dropping the sign of the x² term in ln(1 + x) and getting +1/2

threads.echo: Near 0 a function and its polynomial series are the same object written differently, and the polynomial form makes the 0/0 cancel out.

subtopics.title: Implicit differentiation, related rates of change and optimisation
subtopics.guide: Implicit differentiation of relations in x and y, related rates of change linked by the chain rule, and optimisation problems, including cases where the best value is at an endpoint of the domain rather than at a stationary point.

skills.name: Find dy/dx by implicit differentiation
examTypes: Find dy/dx in terms of x and y for x² + 3xy + y² = 11
Given that y³ + x eʸ = 4, find an expression for dy/dx
Show that dy/dx = (y − 2x)/(2y − x) for the curve x² − xy + y² = 7

methods.name: Differentiate each term with respect to x
methods.summary: Differentiate every term, multiplying by dy/dx whenever a function of y is differentiated, use the product rule on terms like xy, then collect the dy/dx terms and factorise.

methods.name: Rearrange for y first
methods.summary: When y can be isolated (e.g. xy = 6 gives y = 6/x), differentiate explicitly and compare; usually only possible for simple relations.

misconceptions: Differentiating y² as 2y with no dy/dx
Differentiating xy as x dy/dx only (or as dy/dx), missing the y from the product rule
Differentiating the constant on the right as itself instead of 0

threads.echo: Implicit differentiation asks how fast each term changes as x increases by one, with y changing at rate dy/dx along the curve.

skills.name: Use implicit differentiation for gradients, tangents and normals
examTypes: Find the equation of the tangent to x² + y² − 4xy = 13 at the point (−1, 2)
Find the coordinates of the points on the curve where the tangent is horizontal
Find the gradient of the normal at the point where x = 0

methods.name: Substitute the point before rearranging
methods.summary: Differentiate implicitly, put in the x and y values straight away, and solve the resulting linear equation for dy/dx.

methods.name: Find dy/dx in general first
methods.summary: Rearrange for dy/dx in terms of x and y, then substitute; needed when looking for horizontal (numerator = 0) or vertical (denominator = 0) tangents.

methods.name: Check on the graph
methods.summary: Graph the curve (or its explicit branches) and the tangent to confirm they touch at the point.

misconceptions: Setting the denominator of dy/dx to zero to find horizontal tangents (that gives vertical ones)
